_note: The exam of plain lines, made by scripts/auto/exam_lines.py build from the blind checks of plain lines on file. An item is one plain line beside the checked claim it was written from ('claims': the claim as the blind checker saw it). good: the checker left the line as written, or it is the checker's corrected line; not good: the line as first written, which the checker changed because it said something the claim does not carry ('what': the checker's reason; 'now': the corrected line). Lines changed for form only are left out.

check-2026-11-13r/657:cl_opi_supervised_: In the City of Vancouver, Canada, in 2001–2005, the opening of North America's first medically supervised injection site (the supervised injecting facility in the Downtown Eastside, opened on 21 September 2003, where people inject drugs obtained beforehand under the supervision of health professionals who give emergency care, including oxygen and naloxone; by an earlier count, heroin made up about 40% of the injections there, powder cocaine about 30% and methamphetamine 5%) is associated with a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 metres of the site than in the rest of the city, in one before-and-after study without adjustment for anything else. Within 500 metres there were 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before the opening (22,066 person-years; 253.8 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI 187.3 to 320.3) and 33 in the 2.3 years after (19,991 person-years; 165.1, 108.8 to 221.4), a fall of 35.0% (0.0% to 57.7%; rate difference 88.7 per 100,000 person-years, 1.6 to 175.8, p=0.048), about 6 fewer deaths a year (editors' calculation: about 20.6 a year before and 14.5 after); in the rest of the city there were 113 deaths (1,479,792 person-years; 7.6 per 100,000) and 88 (1,271,246; 6.9), a fall of 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%; p=0.490). The test of the difference between the two falls in absolute terms (rate differences; Breslow-Day) gave p=0.049, which the summary calls a significant interaction and the results describe as heterogeneity that might be present; the relative falls (rate ratios 0.65 and 0.91) do not differ significantly (p about 0.20; editors' calculations). The rates rest on census populations interpolated between 2001 and 2006: the population of city blocks within 500 metres rose 14% from 2001 to 2005, which the authors link to more supportive housing, and with the population held at its 2001 level the fall near the site was 30% and not statistically significant (no interval or p value given), although a block-by-block test still showed an overall fall with either population (15 of 22 blocks with deaths fell; p=0.039 both ways). In census tracts, falls were larger nearer the site, minimal beyond about 500 metres and negligible beyond 1 km. Deaths were counted by the place of death, not by use of the site, and no individual was followed (Marshall et al., 2011, a retrospective population-based study of all 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service, 89 of them, 30.7%, within 500 metres and 201 farther away). The coroners recorded opioids as contributing to 156 of the 290 deaths and cocaine to 175 (editors' sums from Table 1; a death can involve both), with no significant change in the drugs involved in either area; the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors could not adjust for neighbourhood changes because Statistics Canada suppressed area characteristics; they report no evidence of changes in drug supply or purity, drug-use patterns, methadone treatment, policing or migration, partly from other studies; one spike of deaths from stolen powdered methadone, after the opening; and police referral of people injecting in public to the site throughout; they state that confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded and that the area-level design calls for caution. High overdose mortality in Vancouver in the 1990s led to the site's opening in the Downtown Eastside; it had 12 injection seats, over 500 supervised injections a day and about 5,000 people who inject drugs nearby, and an earlier study had recorded no deaths inside it. The authors (funded by Vancouver Coastal Health, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research; three of the five also wrote earlier reports of the site's evaluation, which was first funded by Health Canada) call such facilities safe and effective in the discussion, and conclude that they should be considered for assessment where injection drug use is prevalent. A published letter (Christian et al., 2012) argues that the decline owes much to starting in 2001, a year in which, it says, heroin was far more available and deaths more common than in any later year, and that police added in 2003 to 12 city blocks around the site, where it says most of the deaths behind the fall lay (48 to 66 officers, still deployed when it wrote, by an unnamed personal communication), are the most likely cause of any real fall; its own data are yearly death counts, not rates, plotted without values for British Columbia, Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside, all larger areas than the study's (editors' reading of the plot, approximate: Vancouver about 89 deaths in 2001, 49 in 2002 and 56 in 2005; the Downtown Eastside about 31, 27 and 37 in the same years). None of the three papers it cites on heroin and policing, all now on file, measured heroin purity or availability directly (Kerr et al., 2007, and Wood et al., 2006, which it dates 2004, cited for the 2001 point; Wood et al., 2004, cited for policing). The authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012) answers that the letter's Downtown Eastside figures cover the whole local health area (about 400 city blocks, against the study's 41) and, by its account, all drug-induced deaths, suicides included, as counts rather than rates; cites the team's own reports that daily heroin use stayed stable from 2001 to 2005, and a police evaluation for the crackdown having ended within weeks of the opening, so that any displacement would, it argues, have lowered deaths near the site before the opening; and reports a fall of 36% among the deaths with signs of injection at the scene (85% of the 89 near the site), with no count, interval or comparison area; it does not reanalyse the study from 2002, answer the fall in reported non-fatal overdoses that the letter cites from the team's earlier work (Kerr et al., 2007), or give the share of deaths without signs of injection in the rest of the city. These three papers describe the background; only the 2006 paper reports overdose deaths, for British Columbia as a whole. In a Vancouver cohort of 1,587 people who inject drugs, enrolled from 1996 to 2004 and interviewed every 6 months (12,030 interviews), the yearly share who reported a non-fatal overdose of any drug in the previous 6 months (12 months, by the letter) was 21% in 1997 and 6% in 2004, with the largest step between about 12% in 2001 and about 5% in 2002, before the site opened, and about 5% to 7% from 2002 to 2004 (read from a figure, approximate; yearly denominators not printed; the figures are not broken down by area); its authors suggest that reduced heroin supply may have played a role and that expanded methadone treatment may also be involved (the letter says they clearly point to supply), had no measure of supply and could not take drug purity into account (Kerr et al., 2007). The study's before period began on 1 January 2001 and so includes that higher year, as does its comparison with the rest of the city. The 2006 paper, by three of the study's authors, compared markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada before and after an Australian heroin shortage that it dates from about January 2001, as yearly averages without tests or a comparison series: overdose deaths in British Columbia (vital statistics, any drug) 297 in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03; ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside 674 against 370 a year (fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03); heroin seized for Canada 184 kg against 67 kg. In its yearly figures (editors' reading, approximate), deaths fell mostly before 2001 (about 399 in 1998, 272 in 1999 and 218 in 2000), were about the same in 2001 (221) and lower in 2002 and 2003 (169 and 186); naloxone use fell in every fiscal year after 1998–99 (about 840 to 350), its last two years inside the study's before period; and seizures were lower in every year from 2001 (about 94, 46 and 60 kg) than in any year before. In the same Vancouver cohort (1,587 participants, May 1996 to December 2004), self-reported daily heroin injection was 36.5% in 1997/98, 32.6% in 1999/00, 23.3% in 2001/02 and 20.8% in 2003/04, by two-year period (adjusted odds ratio 0.55, 0.50 to 0.61, for 2001–04 against 1996–2000). It measured neither purity nor price, has no figures after 2003 (2004 for the cohort) and none for the study's areas, and its authors infer a fall in supply from these markers; it places 2001 in the low period, with deaths that year about level with 2000 and seizures about half of 2000's and twice 2002's. The study cites it for daily heroin injecting of 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting of 17% and 15% and stable methadone use, none of which is in it; the reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same authors and a 2009 web report for that point, neither on file (Wood et al., 2006). The police crackdown in the Downtown Eastside began on 7 April 2003, inside the before period; in its first three months, discarded syringes fell within a block of Main and Hastings (monthly averages 1,082 to 585) and rose in the rest of the Downtown Eastside (784 to 1,253), the only area counted (the letter places the rise in other areas of Vancouver), more cohort members living there said police had changed where they used drugs, and reported daily heroin use and heroin prices did not differ detectably; the paper does not say how long the crackdown lasted (Wood et al., 2004). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

Residents of the City of Vancouver as the denominator (census populations; on average about 8,100 before and 8,800 after within 500 metres of the site, editors' calculation from person-years), with the 290 deaths ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses by the British Columbia Coroners Service from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 (229 men; median age 40), counted by place of death; the site's neighbourhood, the Downtown Eastside, had about 5,000 people who inject drugs, as cited

Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an unadjusted before-and-after comparison with changes at the same time) and one for imprecision (few deaths, an interval reaching no fall, a borderline difference between the areas in absolute falls only, and a fall near the site that loses significance when the population is held constant): very low. Rated as worded: an association between the opening of one site and a larger fall in coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 m than elsewhere in Vancouver in 2001–2005; not that supervised injection sites reduce deaths, nor that people who used the site were less likely to die, which the study did not measure. The authors' discussion calls such facilities safe and effective; 'safe' rests on other studies they cite, not on these data, and their conclusion asks that sites be considered for assessment. The drugs: opioids contributed to about half of the deaths and cocaine to about 6 in 10 (editors' sums; a death can involve both), and people at the site injected mostly heroin and powder cocaine; the paper does not mention fentanyl, so it says nothing about a supply in which fentanyl is common. Status single study. Now read against the published letter (Christian et al., 2012) and the authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012), from their PDFs (METHODS §2.3): rating and status unchanged. The letter disputes the cause of the fall, which the claim does not assert, and names two further changes at the same time (a police operation around the site in 2003 and a fall in heroin supply around 2001), now in the statement; it is entered as argument, attributed, since its own data are counts for areas larger than the study's, its police figures rest on an unnamed personal communication and its other figures are second-hand. The study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the 2001 start, and in the letter's own figure the drop from 2001 to 2002 is large in the Vancouver series (about 89 to 49 deaths) and small in the Downtown Eastside series (about 31 to 27; editors' reading). The reply answers the points on area, kinds of death and rates, and adds one restricted reanalysis of the same records (36%, no interval or comparison area), which is not independent replication; its answers on heroin and policing rest on its authors' own reports and a police evaluation, not read here; it leaves the 2001 start, the non-fatal overdose trend and the share of deaths without signs of injection elsewhere unanswered; and its call for such facilities to be central to responses goes beyond the paper's own call for assessment. Which deaths the letter's Downtown Eastside series counts cannot be settled from the two letters (a coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths, by the letter; vital statistics including suicides, by the reply). Also read against the two papers the letter cites that are on file (Kerr et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2004), from their PDFs: rating and status unchanged. Neither measured heroin availability or purity or overdose deaths, and neither reports figures for the study's two areas (within 500 m of the site and the rest of the city), so neither tests the letter's explanations or the study's association. The cohort's fall in self-reported non-fatal overdoses, largest between 2001 and 2002, is a fact about the background in the study's before period, which began in 2001: it fits the letter's point that 2001 was a high year in that cohort, but the study's comparison with the rest of the city shares the same start, the cohort is not split by area, and its authors' reasons (heroin supply, methadone) are suggestions without data on supply. The crackdown began inside the before period, and in its first three months more people living in the Downtown Eastside reported changing where they used drugs and discarded syringes shifted from its core to the rest of the neighbourhood; whether added police stayed after the opening (the letter) or left within weeks of it (the reply), neither paper shows. The letter departs from both papers in places: the cohort's question covered 6 months, not 12; its authors offer reduced supply only as a possible reason, alongside methadone; and the syringe counts that rose were in the rest of the Downtown Eastside, the only area counted, not in other areas of Vancouver (the paper's own abstract speaks of displacement into adjacent areas of the city). Not contested (§6.4): the letter offers no reanalysis of the study's areas and does not change the reading of the claim as worded, an unadjusted association near one site. Also read against the letter's other source on heroin, which the study itself cites too (Wood et al., 2006, dated 2004 in the letter), from its PDF: rating and status unchanged. It is a comparison of periods by three of the study's authors (card sc_wood_2006, ROBINS-E high): it measured no heroin purity, price or availability directly, has no figures after 2003 (2004 for its cohort) and none for the study's two areas, so it tests neither the letter's explanation nor the study's association. Its yearly figures fill in the background. Across British Columbia, overdose deaths fell mostly from 1998 to 2000, were about level in 2001 and lower in 2002 and 2003, which partly fits the letter's point that 2001 had more deaths than later years, but places most of the fall before the study began; the paper itself counts 2001 in the period of reduced supply, and in its figures 2001 was about level with 2000 for deaths and about half of 2000 for seizures, so it shows 2001 neither as clearly high nor as clearly low. Ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside fell in every fiscal year to 2002–03, a fall under way in the site's neighbourhood during the before period that the study's unadjusted two-period comparison cannot separate from the opening, although whether the rest of the city fell alike is not shown. Self-reported daily heroin injection in the team's cohort was lower in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000. The paper does not contain the figures the study cites it for (daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%, stable methadone use), which leaves the study's statement that drug use stayed constant without a source that can be checked here; the reply's sources for the same point are other reports, not on file. These points add to the reasons for the existing risk-of-bias downgrade rather than changing it, and the rating is already very low. Later evaluations of the same site, on the project's PDF request list, are not on file; the claim must still be read against them before it leaves draft (METHODS §2.3).
check-2026-11-13r/657:cl_fent_touch: In emergency responders such as police officers and paramedics, evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how often, incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues on the skin causes opioid toxicity (an overdose): no source on file measured responders' exposure or blood levels or counted poisonings among exposed responders, and none of the four, a position statement and three descriptive studies, documents a confirmed case. A 2017 position statement of two North American clinical-toxicology societies, the American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology (AACT) (Moss et al., 2017: eight authors from poison centres, universities, hospitals and a public health institute in the USA and Canada; the recommendations rest on the opinion and clinical experience of a task force of ACMT members and a literature search by the authors; reviewed by an ACMT committee, its board and its members and approved by both societies' boards; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; filed here as a narrative review, so its figures are second-hand and no search method is given), measured no exposure, blood level or responder, and says that its recommendations mainly represent the consensus opinion of experts because data are limited. The two societies judged the risk of clinically significant exposure for responders to be extremely low, and incidental absorption through the skin unlikely (in the recommendations, very unlikely) to cause opioid toxicity. They wrote that they had not seen reports of responders developing signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact, and that the reports they cite (a 2016 warning of the US Drug Enforcement Administration, with two 2017 news reports cited for responders' concern) described nonspecific symptoms, such as dizziness or a feeling that the body was shutting down, without objective signs such as slowed breathing; the incidents are not examined one by one and no count of exposures is given, so the statement could not have detected how often poisoning happens. Their reasoning is arithmetic for fentanyl, not measurement: with both palms covered by fentanyl skin patches, which are made to deliver the drug, about 14 minutes would be needed to absorb 100 micrograms, an amount the statement treats as a high dose without saying why it was chosen (editors' check: 425 micrograms an hour at the stated steady-state rate); they argue that powder or tablets on the skin are taken up more slowly than from a patch and can be brushed or washed off, so that toxicity, if it occurred, would not develop rapidly. At the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed), and the statement says that fentanyl's very low vapour pressure suggests evaporation from standing powder is not a practical concern. Splashes to the eyes or mouth are treated as a real route (absorption across mucous membranes more than 30 times that across skin, as stated; one case report of a veterinarian who became drowsy after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, where the authors say the part played by carfentanil is unclear). No estimate is given for carfentanil, described as 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals, or for any other analogue, although the conclusions cover them; the statement says that the analogues' physical properties suggest a potential for skin absorption and that pharmacological data on other analogues are limited. It concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. It holds that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug, and it still recommends nitrile gloves for routine handling, washing skin with water rather than with alcohol-based sanitizers, and, in the unusual case of significant airborne powder, a properly fitted N95 respirator or P100 mask, which it judges likely to give reasonable protection (its summary says an N95 gives sufficient protection in exceptional circumstances with drug particles or droplets in the air); it adds that individual practitioners may differ. The first data, all descriptive, also find no confirmed case, and none could have found how often one occurs. A review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020: eight authors from an emergency medicine department at Johns Hopkins University, published as an editorial in the journal that carried the position statement, with the statement's last author as its senior author; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared) searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online news from North America published from January 2012 to March 2018: of 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 were on the topic and 214 described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid, and none of the 214 described a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together. Only one incident, in 2016, mentioned any laboratory test of an exposed responder, a urine result reported as traces of opiates, which the authors explain probably came from an opiate screen, a test that does not detect fentanyl or its analogues and, in urine, reflects exposure over the previous several days rather than at the time. The unit is the article, not the incident (distinct incidents are not counted), each article was read by one of five reviewers against criteria the paper does not define, and only the three-part combination is reported, so the zero shows that the news did not report confirmation, mainly because testing was almost never mentioned, not what happened to the responders. A Health Hazard Evaluation by the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH; Jackson et al., 2018) reconstructed one incident in early 2018 from records and from interviews four months later: during a vehicle search, white powder from a locked box blew into the faces of two officers, who within minutes reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion, and a colleague gave one of them naloxone for what was described as shallow breathing and fading consciousness; emergency medical services then found both alert and oriented with normal oxygen saturation, and in the emergency department both had normal-sized pupils and normal heart and breathing rates, neither had any laboratory test, and both went home after more than an hour without symptoms. A field test of the seized substances was reported positive for fentanyl, but the state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC and no fentanyl or other opioid. Nothing was measured on the officers or in the air, the powder reached their faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and their perceived risk was not assessed; the clinicians who examined them saw no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity, and NIOSH considers it possible that the non-specific symptoms reflected milder toxicity from some drug. In the same report NIOSH states, as its own position and citing the position statement among its sources, that a brief touch of fentanyl powder, or of an analogue, is not expected to be toxic when visible powder is quickly removed. A later NIOSH article (Chiu et al., 2019: seven NIOSH authors, two of whom also wrote that report; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; read as its author manuscript) summarizes two other incidents that NIOSH investigated, from 2017 and 2018, chosen to illustrate different scenarios; neither is the incident of that report. In the first, during a traffic stop, wind blew powder from a container onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, who cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; within 5 minutes the officer felt disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision, and ambulance staff washed the skin with water and found the officer alert, with pupils of 4 mm, a breathing rate of 17 a minute and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no laboratory test was done, the officer was discharged with an assessment of chemical exposure, and the laboratory later found fentanyl with methamphetamine in the powder left in the container. In the second, four officers became lightheaded or dizzy, among other symptoms, after a call to a hotel room with drug powders in view: three who had entered the room, about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began, and one who never entered, 30 to 45 minutes after handling a camera and other items from the room that showed no visible contamination; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave naloxone; none was reported to have depressed breathing (one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department), all were alert with no documented constricted pupils, and their urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative; the laboratory found fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in the room. Nothing was measured in the air, on surfaces or skin, or in blood, and perceived risk was not assessed. The authors judge that no officer's effects were consistent with severe opioid toxicity, consider breathing in, the lining of the eyes, nose or mouth, swallowing and the skin all possible routes, and read the one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids played a substantial part, an inference from one uncontrolled observation in an officer whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; like NIOSH's report, they state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic when visible contamination is promptly removed, and they add that alcohol-based hand sanitizer may increase absorption. None of these studies can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and three incidents, investigated because officers fell ill, give no rate. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the absence of a confirmed case only).

Emergency responders (law enforcement and emergency medical services) in North America who may meet fentanyl or fentanyl analogues as powder, tablets or liquid on calls, at crime scenes or in drug raids: as considered in a 2017 position statement, which studied no responders, exposures or cases; as reported in 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) that described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid; and two sheriff's department officers in one incident in early 2018, investigated afterwards by NIOSH, and five police officers in two other incidents of 2017 and 2018, also investigated afterwards by NIOSH (Chiu et al., 2019)

Incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues: on the skin (the question here), and also airborne powder breathed in, splashes to the eyes or mouth, and being near the drug; reasoned from pharmacokinetic data in the position statement, as reported in news articles (routes recorded but not reported), and, in the NIOSH incident, white powder of unknown composition blown into two officers' faces; in the two incidents of Chiu et al., powder blown onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, which the laboratory later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine, and a hotel room with drug powders in view, with items from it handled elsewhere; no source measured any exposure

None in any source: the position statement collected no data, and its worked arithmetic takes as its reference the time needed to absorb 100 micrograms of fentanyl through the skin, or the exposure needed to reach a dose of 100 micrograms from the air, an amount it does not justify; the news review and the incident investigations had no comparison group

Clinically significant opioid toxicity in the responder (objective signs such as slowed breathing or a lowered level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety; in the news review, a confirmed exposure (an article describing a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together); in the NIOSH incidents, symptoms and clinical findings in emergency medical service and emergency department records (with urine drug screens, unable to detect fentanyl, in four officers), and forensic analysis of the substances seized

No measured rate or count of poisonings. ACMT and AACT position (Moss et al., 2017): risk of clinically significant exposure extremely low; no reports seen of responders with signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact; incidental skin absorption unlikely (summary) or very unlikely (recommendations) to cause toxicity. Worked arithmetic, fentanyl only: both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, delivery 2.5 micrograms per cm2 per hour at steady state), about 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms (editors' check: 170 cm2 × 2.5 = 425 micrograms an hour, so 14.1 minutes); patches take 3–13 hours to give a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 hours to peak; at the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed); vapour pressure 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa. Mucous membranes: more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case report of drowsiness after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, its cause unclear to the authors. No estimate for carfentanil (10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals) or any other analogue. Respiratory protection: an N95 respirator or P100 mask likely to give reasonable protection against significant airborne powder (recommendations); an N95 sufficient in exceptional circumstances with particles or droplets in the air (summary). Herman et al. (2020), English-language North American print and online news (LexisNexis), January 2012 to March 2018: 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 relevant (editors: 72%), 214 describing a specific responder exposure (editors: 21% of relevant); 0 of 214 with a plausible route, consistent symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing together; any laboratory testing of an exposed person mentioned for 1 incident (2 articles; editors: 0.9% of 214), an opiate urine result; distinct incidents not counted, and no count reported for any single criterion. Jackson et al. check-2026-11-13r/657:cl_lsd_chromosomes: In people studied from 1967 to 1970, both people given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings and people who reported taking LSD outside them, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD, compared with no LSD or with each person's own sample from before LSD, changes chromosome breakage. Six of the primary studies have been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), among them the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage after LSD; the others, including the later and larger studies of those two laboratories and the study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968), are known only through one 1971 narrative review in Science (Dishotsky et al., 1971; figures second-hand; no search method or selection criteria stated; supported in part by the State of California Department of Mental Hygiene and by Mendocino State Hospital, where two of the authors worked; its tables include the authors' own unpublished study, and its second author, W. D. Loughman, was the first author of one of the negative studies, Loughman et al., 1967). What these studies measured was breaks seen under a microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells taken from the blood and made to divide in a culture dish, counted as breaks per cell in some studies and as the share of cells with any aberration in others, in groups of 1 to 46 people, by laboratories whose breakage rates in unexposed controls ranged from 0% to 11.9%; most breaks recorded were of a kind that the review's authors say mostly arises from the culture procedure itself, and they limit their own conclusion to damage detectable by the methods then available. The concern began with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), as Tjio et al. (1969) note, mainly a study of cells in a dish, not of people: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors, whose results were pooled, was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 conditions of concentration and exposure time, against 0.037 (34 breaks in 925 cells) in untreated cultures from six people, with no statistical test of the difference (the review nonetheless lists it as significant) and, in the paper's own Table 1, no steady rise with concentration; its one patient, a man given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy who had also been treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, had 12% breakage in 200 cells 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7% of untreated cultures from other people, with no sample from before LSD (the same laboratory's later report lists, as its case 37, a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells; he matches this patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, but neither paper says whether he is the same man). Later in 1967 the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage, both read in full, compared people who had taken LSD with people who had not, with coded slides but no samples from before LSD and no statistical comparison of the groups in either paper. Irwin and Egozcue (1967) found on average 23.6 breaks per 100 cells in 8 men who reported taking LSD an estimated 4 to 200 times (its source not stated; some had also taken cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, not counted) against 11.9 in 9 volunteers who had not taken it (editors' calculation; 95% interval of the difference about 3.7 to 19.7), with overlapping ranges, no women in the LSD group, and the two highest control rates in people with x-ray exposure. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) found 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD, every one of whom had also taken other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15, phenothiazines 10) and whose recruitment and source of LSD are not described, against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls without drugs, after two controls with 31.0 and 14.0 were left out for a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (5.4 breaks per 100 cells with them, pooled; 6.5 as the mean of the 14 controls' rates); yet 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (three of them chlorpromazine, two of them boys aged 9) had similar rates, 12.6 on average, no different from the LSD patients (editors' calculation; the paper makes no such comparison); and 4 children exposed to LSD before birth had 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults. Two other small cross-sectional studies found no excess: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent use of illicit LSD (7 of them also amphetamines), scored by someone who did not know their drug histories, against none in 112 cells from one concurrent control and 1 in 561 cells from 18 earlier controls of the same laboratory (Loughman et al., 1967); and 2.2 breaks per 100 cells (21 in 937) in 4 psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and 1.5 (14 in 914) in 4 patients given LSD in treatment, against 1.6 (15 in 950) in 4 hospital volunteers, with each sample cultured in two laboratories and blinding of the scorers not reported (Sparkes et al., 1968); groups this small cannot exclude a modest rise. (1969), sampled 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis before and 1 to 10 days after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with coded samples scored by one reader who did not know whether a sample came before or after LSD: the share of cells with chromosome aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not a significant change (P = 0.3; 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 percentage points, editors' calculation); 3 patients had large rises (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%), and the 2 of them who could be retested were back within the normal range 71 and 229 days later (one still 2.32 points above his own earlier rate); there was no untreated comparison group, and 31 of the 32 had been given other medicines in hospital before their first sample. Cohen, Marinello, et al. and Tjio et al. both used LSD supplied by Sandoz Pharmaceuticals. What these designs can show is limited: cells in a dish are not people, blood cells are not sperm or egg cells (none of these studies examined those), and pharmaceutical LSD given in hospital is not street LSD of unknown content. In the review's tallies, of 310 people in 21 reports from 17 laboratories, at most 18 of 126 given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%) had breakage above their control group's average (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient is counted among the first; if he is also Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s case 37, he is counted among the second as well). Among people given pharmaceutical LSD, the review's comparisons with unexposed controls found raised breakage in at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), all but one (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient) reported by one team whose methods the review's authors criticize (as few as 3 of 61, 4.9%, leaving out that team's incomplete data); in 56 people tested before and after, 6 (10.7%) had raised breakage afterwards, 3 of them after LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968, as the review describes it) and 1 with a viral infection, and the review says the 5 of these 6 who were retested 2 weeks to 7.67 months later were back at their earlier rates (in Tjio et al.'s own figures, one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate); only the intravenous study (3 people) showed a significant group change (1.0% to 4.78%), and in Tjio et al.'s study, which the review counts as 37 patients, the 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before, reported with the 32 patients, went from 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from the paper's own Table 4, editors' calculation), not significantly. In cells exposed to LSD in a dish, 6 of 9 studies found more breaks, mostly at concentrations or exposure times the review's authors judge unreachable in people, and in one study aspirin raised breakage about as much as LSD (9.6% and 10.2% of cells, against 5.0% in untreated cells); in Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s cultures, 7.7 to 17.5 breaks per 100 cells against 3.9, with no statistical test and no rise across a 10,000-fold range of concentrations. On cancer, the review found no significant research, only three case reports of leukaemia or other cancers in about four years, and it says that, as of then, there appeared to be no definite evidence that LSD causes cancer. On birth defects, no malformation had been reported after pharmaceutical LSD and six after illicit LSD (several of the mothers also used other drugs), which the review's authors say may be coincidence; of 14 children exposed to illicit LSD before birth, 10 had raised breakage and all were healthy without birth defects (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s 4 children, 2 of them with high rates against adult controls and none with obvious abnormalities, belong to a report the review does not cite for this count); and in a series of 148 pregnancies, spontaneous abortions occurred in 37% when parents had used both pharmaceutical and illicit LSD, against 15% with pharmaceutical LSD alone and 20% in the general population, but only 12 of the pregnancies involved LSD during gestation and one woman accounted for 5 of the 10 abortions in the combined group. Animal results were inconsistent: in fruit flies, mutations appeared only at concentrations the review's authors call extremely high; malformations were seen in some mouse strains but not others; and of four pregnant rhesus monkeys given repeated injections at 100 or more times the usual human experimental dose, two delivered stillborn infants with facial deformities and one infant died at a month, which the review calls preliminary but suggestive. In the editors' reading, the review authors' closing statement that they believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man goes beyond this evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.

People whose blood cells were examined from 1967 to 1970. Read in full: cultured white blood cells from two donors and one man treated with LSD in psychotherapy (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967); 8 men reporting LSD use against 9 volunteers without it (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967); 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD, 12 drug-free controls (2 more left out), 4 children exposed before birth and cultured cells from 6 donors (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use against 19 laboratory controls (Loughman et al., 1967); three groups of 4, namely hospital volunteers, psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and patients given LSD in treatment (Sparkes et al., 1968); and 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before (Tjio et al., 1969). As summarized in one narrative review: 21 reports from 17 laboratories with 310 people, 126 given pharmaceutical (pure) LSD in medical or research settings (many of them patients, some treated with psychiatric medicines) and 184 who had used illicit drugs sold as LSD (nearly all of whom also used other drugs), in groups of 1 to 46 people, 56 of the 126 tested before and after LSD; children exposed before birth reported separately (14 exposed to illicit LSD); also cultured cells, fruit flies, a fungus, rodents and monkeys

Pharmaceutical LSD given under supervision (one to three treatments in the before-and-after studies, by mouth except in one study of 3 people given it into a vein; more in some comparison studies, for example 15 sessions in Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient), or self-reported use of LSD outside medical settings, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, of unknown content and strength (the source is not stated in Irwin & Egozcue, 1967, or Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); in laboratory studies, LSD added to cultured cells

Unexposed control groups (breakage rates of 0% to 11.9% between laboratories), each person's own sample from before LSD (with no untreated group sampled at the same times in the largest study), untreated cultures in the cell studies, or, in one study, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967)

Chromosome breakage, mostly chromatid-type breaks, counted under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture (as breaks per cell or as the share of cells with an aberration, which differ between studies); also, as reported in the review, case reports of cancer, birth defects and spontaneous abortions after LSD, mutations in fruit flies and a fungus, and malformations in rodents and monkeys

Primary studies read in full. Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors: 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 LSD conditions against 0.037 (34 of 925 cells) in untreated cultures, no statistical test (384 breaks in 2678 treated cells, 0.143 per cell, editors' sum); one patient 12% in 200 cells, no sample from before LSD. Irwin & Egozcue (1967): breaks per 100 cells 12.0 to 38.0 in 8 men reporting LSD use against 7.0 to 25.0 in 9 volunteers without it; means 23.6 against 11.9 (378 of 1600 and 215 of 1800 cells; difference 11.7, 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7, editors' calculation; the review prints 23.4% against 11.0% in its text and 11.9% in its table); P < .05 for 6 of 8 and 1 of 9 people, test not named. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967): 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 drug-free controls, no test (difference 9.3, 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3, editors' calculation; with the 2 controls left out after a viral illness included, 5.4 pooled (161 in 2974) and a per-person mean of 6.5, a difference in per-person means of 6.6, 1.5 to 11.7); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD 12.6 (mean of six rates; 161 in 1361 cells), not different from the LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84, editors' calculation); 4 children exposed before birth 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults; cells in a dish from 6 donors 7.7 to 17.5 against 3.9 (1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells, editors' sum; the review lists 8725 cells), no concentration-response, no test. Loughman et al. (1967): 0 chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people (95% limits 0.0% to 0.5%) against 0 of 112 (1 concurrent control), 1 of 561 (0.2%; 18 earlier controls) and 11 of 1569 (0.7%; published controls), not significant. Sparkes et al. (1968): breaks per 100 cells 2.2 (21/937; LSD taken privately, 4 people), 1.5 (14/914; LSD in treatment, 4) and 1.6 (15/950; controls, 4); cells with a break 1.4%, 1.4% and 1.5%; not significant (with 4 against 4 the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.029, editors' calculation). Tjio et al. (1969), 32 patients before and after one dose: cells with aberrations 4.28% to 5.91% (+1.63 points; P = 0.3; lower dose level, 11 patients, 4.05% to 9.26%, P = 0.15; higher, 21 patients, 4.39% to 4.16%, P = 0.8); editors' calculation: 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 points, 18 rose, 12 fell, 2 unchanged; 3 rises of more than 4 points (2.44% to 23.08%, 9.50% to 43.92%, 1.48% to 14.16%), 2 retested at 4.76% (71 days) and 1.48% (229 days); 5 volunteers with earlier illicit use 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from Table 4, editors' calculation), not significant. Dishotsky et al. (1971), counts without intervals: breakage above control means in at most 18 of 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%; 45.98%, 80 of 174, without one study's incomplete data); 18 of the 108 people reported with damage had pharmaceutical LSD (16.67%). Illicit-LSD studies: 80 of 86 raised in two early teams' studies (for example 18.76% against 9.03% in 46 people, and 13.2% against 3.8% in 18); none beyond the general population in nine other teams' studies (88 people, editors' sum). Pharmaceutical LSD compared with unexposed controls: at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), as few as 3 of 61 (4.9%). Before and after: 6 of 56 raised (10.7%); group averages 5.7% to 4.9% (10 people), 0.0% to 0.0% (6), 2.81% to 3.57% (5) and 4.28% to 5.91% (32), not significant; 1.0% to 4.78% after intravenous LSD (3 people), significant; 50 of 53 given LSD by mouth (94.3%) showed no increase. Other drugs: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD 12.6% against 13.2% in 18 patients with LSD and other drugs, not significantly different by the review's own comparison (the paper reports none; editors' check above). In vitro: 6 of 9 studies positive; in one study LSD 10.2%, aspirin 9.6% and ergonovine 10.0% against 5.0% in control cells. Pregnancies: spontaneous abortion 37% (pharmaceutical plus illicit LSD), 15% (pharmaceutical only), 20% (general population), in 148 pregnancies with 12 exposed during gestation.

Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies had been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); later that day the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage were read in full too (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), without a change of rating. The human primary studies are observational, four cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture studies are preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies that found no excess (8 people; groups of 4) cannot exclude a modest rise; the two that found about two and three times the controls' break rates (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12) had no samples from before LSD, did not describe recruitment and reported no statistical comparison, and in the larger of them every LSD patient had taken other drugs or medicines and 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so the excess cannot be attributed to LSD; and the cell studies reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. Of the human studies that reported raised breakage, Irwin & Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) are now read in full; they leave the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments as they were, with the explanation of the positive findings now resting partly on first-hand data. The study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968) and the two laboratories' later studies enter only as the review describes them. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test; Irwin and Egozcue print no group means, and their table gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation), not the review's 23.4% and 11.0% (11.9% in its table); Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say where their patients' LSD came from, report no test for their cells in a dish, and their Table 5 sums to 7735 treated cells, not 8725; and the review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose does not fit Irwin and Egozcue's own table, in which the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate in 8 people (editors' calculation). Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say whether their case 37, who matches Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s single patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, is the same man; if so, the review counts him both among people given pharmaceutical LSD and among people exposed to illicit LSD. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many drugs and medicines and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs and medicines, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible, and supported in one study by a small comparison group, but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.
check-2026-11-14/697:cl_xc_psychedelic_b: In adults who chose to attend a ceremony, retreat or other guided session with a classic psychedelic and signed up for online surveys (mostly from Western countries, highly educated, and already leaning towards non-physicalist views beforehand), attending, compared with their own answers about a week before, is associated with modestly stronger agreement with non-physicalist statements 4 weeks and 6 months later; in one randomized trial in depression the shift after psilocybin therapy exceeded the shift after escitalopram only on a one-tailed test; and none of the studies tests whether the beliefs are true. On a questionnaire written for the study, whose main factor groups belief in other realms that can be visited, a unifying principle beyond scientific explanation, panpsychism (mind as a quality of all things), dualism and idealism against materialism and naturalism (Timmermann et al., 2021), the 122 respondents with answers at all three time points (819 in the baseline table and 866 said to have answered at some time point, so about 85 in 100 are missing from these analyses and were not compared with those who stayed) shifted by d = 0.33 at 4 weeks and d = 0.46 at 6 months, and the 53 taking a psychedelic for the first time by d = 0.53 and 0.73; belief in fatalistic determinism rose at 4 weeks (d = 0.25) but not at 6 months. Positions moved both ways: of respondents classed as 'hard materialists' at baseline, 24.4% still held that position at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months, most of the others moving to a mixed position or to dualism, while 17.6% and 15.2% of respondents with mixed positions moved to materialism; of those neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% and 54.5% became 'believers' (group sizes not printed, and the samples behind these tables not stated). In an exploratory path model, feeling emotionally in tune with the group during the session predicted the 4-week score (standardized beta 0.22), while mystical-type and visual-effect scores were dropped as not significant. In the same team's double-blind trial in 59 adults with major depression, a 5-item version of the questionnaire shifted after psilocybin therapy (two 25 mg doses and 6 weeks of daily placebo, study condition; d = 0.45) and less after 6 weeks of daily escitalopram given with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin (d = 0.2, p = 0.33, which the authors call no change); the difference between the arms had p = 0.041 one-tailed, about 0.08 two-sided (editors' calculation). In a retrospective online survey by another team, of 1,606 adults recruited because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience, each rating 'before', 'after' and 'now' for their most belief-changing experience in one sitting a mean of 8.2 years after it, the share agreeing that plants can be conscious was 26% before against 61% after, fungi 21% against 56%, insects 33% against 57%, rocks 8% against 26% and the universe 34% against 80%, with 'now' close to 'after'; superstitions (black cats bringing bad luck: 8%, 4% and 3%) and belief in free will (74%, 74% and 73%) did not change meaningfully, and people who remembered a more mystical experience reported larger changes (Nayak & Griffiths, 2022). The cohort cannot separate the drug from the ceremony's group, ritual, teaching and expectations, or show that those who stopped answering changed like those who stayed, and its authors say that views held by co-attendees and by the trial's staff may have passed to participants; the survey, recruited on belief change and relying on memory over years, cannot show how often or how much beliefs change. On truth, the first team writes that judging the value of the positions is beyond its work and that it would be hasty to read its results as favouring them, and the second that persistent beliefs after compelling experiences neither support nor undermine their validity. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.

Adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic and signed up at a study website after online advertisements (819 in the baseline table: mean age 44.4; 55.6% men; 43.8% from the United States and 19.5% from the United Kingdom; 90.7% White; 54.1% with a master's, doctoral or professional degree, editors' sum), of whom 122 answered the belief questions at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months; 59 adults with major depression (30 and 29) in a randomized trial by the same team; and 1,606 adults recruited online by another team because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience (mean age 35.1; 67% men; 89% White; 69% from the United States).

Attending a ceremony or retreat with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD), the substance, amount and setting chosen by the respondents and not reported; in the trial, psilocybin therapy: 25 mg on two dosing days and 6 weeks of daily placebo (study condition); in the survey, a past experience with psilocybin mushrooms (49%), LSD (33%), ayahuasca (7%), N,N-DMT (6%), 5-MeO-DMT (3%) or mescaline-containing cacti (2%), chosen by each respondent as the one that most changed their beliefs.

Each respondent's own answers about a week before the ceremony (no comparison group); in the trial, randomized daily escitalopram for 6 weeks with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin; in the survey, respondents' remembered 'before' beliefs, rated in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'.

Agreement with non-physicalist statements: a 9-item factor (Cronbach's alpha 0.86) of a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study, and 5 of its items in the trial; fatalistic determinism (FAD-Plus items); changes in the position most strongly endorsed; in the survey, the share agreeing that ten kinds of entity can be conscious, five superstition items and one free-will item. Whether any belief is true was not assessed.

Timmermann et al. (2021), cohort, 122 with paired data: non-physicalist factor at 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; at 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (the printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50] cannot be intervals of d; editors' approximate 95% intervals for d, SE = √(1/n + d²/2n), 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65); first-timers (53): d = 0.53 and 0.73; fatalistic determinism d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), not at 6 months. Conversion (Figure 2; group sizes not printed): 'hard materialists' remaining 24.4% (4 weeks) and 22.2% (6 months); dualists remaining 55.5% and 65.2%; none/mixed to materialism 17.6% and 15.2%; panpsychism neutral to believer 57.3% and 54.5%, sceptic to believer 22.6% and 37.8%. Lifetime psychedelic use and baseline factor score: Spearman r = 0.223 (cross-sectional). Path model: emotional synchrony to the 4-week score, beta 0.22. Trial (psilocybin therapy 30, escitalopram 29; 5 items): interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2 (Z = 0.24 gives a one-tailed p of about 0.41, editors' calculation). Nayak & Griffiths (2022), 1,606, % agreeing before, after and now: plants 26, 61, 64; fungi 21, 56, 62; insects 33, 57, 60; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe 34, 80, 82; self 80, 97, 98; no meaningful change for superstitions (black cats 8, 4, 3; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10) or free will (74, 74, 73).

Observational evidence (a prospective cohort without a comparison group and a retrospective survey) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: an association between attending a psychedelic ceremony and modest shifts in stated beliefs among people who kept answering; not that psychedelics cause the shift, that it is specific to psychedelics (escitalopram also moved, d = 0.2, and the difference between the arms was significant only one-tailed), or that it lasts beyond 6 months. The trial is randomized and would start high on its own, but as the only comparison between treatments it rests on 59 patients, a 5-item version and a one-tailed p of 0.041 (about 0.08 two-sided), so it qualifies the claim rather than raising it. Status replicated by the same team: the cohort and the trial are one group's two samples, reported in one paper; the survey from another group agrees in direction but recruited people because their beliefs had changed and relied on recall, so it is not counted as an independent test. Whether the beliefs are true is outside what any of these designs can address, as both teams say.
check-2026-11-14/697:cl_psi_personality: Evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin changes personality. In two small studies with no comparison group for the change, self-rated Openness to experience on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (T scores: population mean 50, SD 10) was a few points higher 1 to 3 months after psilocybin with preparation and support than each person's own score before; the one randomized comparison of personality in these trials found no difference, no paper checked a change against behaviour, and the two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience. In 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers pooled from two double-blind trials at Johns Hopkins (mean age 46; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious or spiritual activities; screening Openness 65.4 and 62.7), Openness was 2.8 T points higher 1 to 2 months after the high-dose session (psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg, study condition; F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023), Neuroticism, Extroversion, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness did not change detectably, and in the 30 whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or a low psilocybin dose Openness did not change after that session (p = 0.48), though the two changes were never compared with each other (MacLean et al., 2011). The rise was in the 30 who met the criterion for a 'complete mystical experience' (+5.7, p = 0.002), not in the other 22 (−1.2), and it correlated with the session's mystical score (r = 0.42); individual changes ranged from about −12 to +36 T points, about 17 of the 51 visible points in the paper's figure lie below zero (about a third of the volunteers scored lower; editors' reading), and without the three largest rises the other 49 would average about +1.3 (editors' approximate calculation, (2.8 × 52 − 84) / 49). At a mean of 16 months the complete-mystical group was 4.2 points above its screening score at p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation) and the others 0.3 below; the change for all participants together was not reported. In the earlier trial that supplied 35 of these volunteers, the randomized comparison of 15 people given psilocybin first with 15 given methylphenidate first found no difference in any personality factor 2 months later (no values printed; Griffiths et al., 2006, as its checked study card reports), a result MacLean et al. do not mention. In 19 adults with treatment-resistant depression given psilocybin 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later with psychological support in an open-label study in London (Erritzoe et al., 2018; its authors include MacLean et al.'s first author), Neuroticism fell from T 76.6 to 70.9 (p = 0.002), Extraversion rose from 31.1 to 37.6 (p < 0.001) and Openness from 52.7 to 57.6 (p = 0.012) at 3 months, Conscientiousness rose at trend level (p = 0.086) and Agreeableness did not change; Neuroticism, Extraversion and Conscientiousness moved from far outside the norms towards them, and the authors say it is hard to infer that the changes, particularly in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are traits rather than states. The Openness rise did not differ between the 7 patients whose depression responded and the 12 whose did not, and no 'peak experience' score related to it, whereas insightfulness during the session went with the Neuroticism and Extraversion changes in uncorrected, exploratory correlations (r = −0.47 and 0.54). All scores are self-ratings by people who knew, or could probably tell, that they had taken psilocybin, in volunteers drawn to a psilocybin study or to a psychedelic treatment; in the 2006 trial, three people close to each volunteer rated a small positive change in behaviour and attitudes after psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, as its card reports), but no paper read related such ratings, or any behaviour, to the personality scores. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.

52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers recruited by community flyers for a study of states of consciousness brought about by psilocybin (35 from a 2006 trial and 17 from a 2011 trial at Johns Hopkins; mean age 46; 22 men and 30 women, editors' sum; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation; screening Openness T 65.4 and 62.7); in the 2006 trial, 30 volunteers randomized to drug order (15 per order); and 19 analysed of 20 adults with moderate to severe treatment-resistant unipolar depression in an open-label study in London (6 women, 13 men; mean age 44.7; five had tried a psychedelic before).

Psilocybin by mouth with preparation and support, as study conditions only: one session at 30 mg/70 kg (in the 2011 trial within four ascending or descending doses with a placebo session), lying down with an eye mask and music, after at least 8 hours of meetings with the session monitors; in the open-label study, 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later, eyes closed with music and two therapists, with integration visits afterwards.

Each person's own personality scores before (screening or baseline), with no concurrent comparison of change in either main study; within the healthy volunteers, people with and without a 'complete mystical experience' (not randomized) and, separately, change after a first session of placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg; in the 2006 trial, people given psilocybin first against people given methylphenidate first (randomized; no values printed).

Self-rated personality on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (240 items; five domains of six facets; T scores from combined-sex norms), 1 to 2 months after the session and about 14 months after the last session (a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session) in the healthy volunteers, and 3 months after in the patients; no behavioural measure and no ratings of personality by others.

MacLean et al. (2011), 52 volunteers, screening to 1–2 months: Openness +2.8 T points, F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10 (editors' calculation: within-person standardized change about 0.32, √(5.47/52)); Neuroticism −0.5 (p = 0.62), Extroversion +0.8 (p = 0.38), Agreeableness +1.7 (F = 2.31, printed p = 0.16; 0.13 by the editors' calculation), Conscientiousness −0.9 (p = 0.28). After a first session without high-dose psilocybin (30): F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48. Complete mystical experience (30) against not (22): F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004; +5.7 (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002) against −1.2 (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39). Mystical score and Openness change r = 0.42, p = 0.002 (editors' 95% CI about 0.17 to 0.62, Fisher z). Follow-up (mean 16 months): complete group +4.2, F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation); others (21) −0.3, p = 0.86; all participants not reported. Figure 1 (editors' reading): changes from about −12 to +36, about 17 of 51 visible points below zero; about +1.3 without the three largest (editors' approximate calculation). Griffiths et al. check-2026-11-14/697:cl_opi_conditioned_: In people who use heroin, evidence is insufficient to say whether taking it in surroundings not linked with past use raises the risk of overdose: the idea comes from a conditioning model of tolerance tested mainly in rats, and the only study in people is a set of 10 overdose survivors' recollections with no comparison. The model, as its author states it (Siegel, 1984, 2005): cues present when a drug is taken, such as the place, the people and the act of taking it, become linked with its effects and come to trigger responses that oppose those effects; these learned responses are part of tolerance, so tolerance should be weaker where the drug has not been taken before. The animal evidence is described by the same author without figures: rats with the same heroin history were more likely to survive a high intravenous dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin than the same dose given in a different environment (Siegel et al., 1982, as described in Siegel, 1984; the 1982 paper itself was not read), and setting-specific tolerance is said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named). The 2005 review also describes, without numbers, two laboratory examples in people that do not involve opioids: more tolerance to alcohol drunk in a familiar beer-flavoured drink than in an unfamiliar blue, peppermint-flavoured one, and more tolerance to a heart effect of caffeine taken in coffee than at the same blood level reached intravenously. check-2026-11-14/698:cl_benzo_stopping_s: Evidence is insufficient to say how often stopping benzodiazepines suddenly leads to seizures or other severe withdrawal reactions, or how much stopping gradually lowers that risk. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews (Lader, 2011, a descriptive review based on a lecture; Brett & Murnion, 2015, a four-page clinical review for prescribers that cites the 2011 review elsewhere), stopping or cutting down after regular use can bring a withdrawal syndrome: the 2011 review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use but only in about 15 to 30 in 100 patients, a figure cited to the author's own 1998 paper on stopping sleeping pills, and that rebound (the original symptoms returning more strongly for a while) is likely when stopping sleeping pills, especially short-acting ones, even after a few nights of use; the 2015 review states, without a reference, that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly. Symptoms listed include anxiety and panic, poor sleep and nightmares, poor memory and concentration, low mood, muscle spasms and aches, numbness and tingling, sweating, and heightened sensitivity to light, sound and touch, with feelings of unreality; the 2011 review says they generally fade within weeks or months, often fluctuating, and both reviews say they can resemble the anxiety or insomnia the drug was taken for. Both reviews describe seizures. The 2011 review lists convulsions (which, it says, may end in death), delirium, psychosis, depression, often severe, and suicidal thoughts among reactions that may follow abrupt stopping but may also occur despite slow tapering, with no frequencies, in a table sourced mainly to a university guide and the author's 1984 monograph (the depression entry to a report of four cases), says many of them are reported anecdotally, with few case series, and that their status remains controversial; it adds that whether withdrawal occurs is related to high doses and long treatment but its severity less closely, and that severe withdrawal may occur despite withdrawal over months or years. The 2015 review states, without a reference or a frequency, that abrupt stopping after 1 to 6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, lists grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping in a box without a source, and describes people without a history of seizures, unstable medical or psychiatric illness or other drug dependence as at lower risk of harm from withdrawal, also without references. The only count of seizures in either review comes from a 1961 study in which 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months were switched to a dummy pill: within 2 to 8 days, 10 developed withdrawal reactions, including depression, psychosis and agitation, and 2 had seizures. Neither review cites a study comparing sudden with gradual stopping for seizures; the 2011 review says the rate at which doses are reduced rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good evidence, and that, in high-dose use as in low-dose dependence, withdrawal can sometimes be severe, with fits and psychotic reactions. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

check-2026-11-15/714:cl_mdma_empathy: In healthy volunteers tested in laboratories, MDMA compared with a dummy pill (placebo) given to the same people on another day, double blind and in random order, is associated with higher self-ratings of feeling loving and friendly and of feeling for people shown in photographs (emotional empathy), but not with better recognition of other people's emotions, which was worse for fear in both studies that found a change: people felt warmer without reading others better. Certainty: low. Status: replicated (two independent teams; the comparison with methamphetamine and the money game rest on one study each). In Chicago, 21 healthy adults aged 18 to 38 (9 women) who had used ecstasy at least twice (15 times on average; 13 fewer than 10 times) each had four sessions at least 5 days apart, in random order: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg and placebo (study conditions), sitting alone in testing rooms (Bedi et al., 2010).
