voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_aya_dmt_entities: In 2,561 adults who answered an anonymous online survey in 2018 after recruitment through websites and forums (for example reddit, dmt-nexus, bluelight and drugs-forum) and by email (mean age 31.9; 77% men; 85% White; 64% living in the USA; a median of 6 lifetime DMT uses), all of whom reported at least one encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity (the study's term) after a 'breakthrough' dose of DMT (defined as one with very strong effects), smoked or vaporized without other substances, and each describing their single most memorable encounter, on average about 4.6 years earlier (editors' calculation from the mean ages now and at the experience), the respondents reported the following (Davis et al., 2020). Only people who reported an encounter could take part, so the survey cannot show how often encounters happen; of the 9,179 eligible people who consented, 4,610 completed the survey and affirmed their answers, and 2,049 of these (editors' sum) were then excluded, by design (103 with a psychotic disorder diagnosis, 1,279 who had taken other substances that may have affected the experience, 457 who took DMT another way) or for duplicate addresses, undisclosed substance use, use of changa or inattentive answers (34 and 176). For 67% the encounter described was their first. They reported mainly seeing (92%) and extrasensory, for example telepathic, contact (85%); 84% reported communication with the entity, 40% two-way and 49% one-way from the entity, most often by telepathy (74%). From a list (all that apply), they called it a being (60%), guide (43%), spirit (39%), alien (39%), helper (34%), angel (16%), elf (14%), religious personage (11%), plant spirit (10%), fairy (8%), clown (6%), demon (6%) or deceased family member (2%), among other labels. During the encounter they felt joy (65%), trust (63%), surprise (61%), love (59%), kindness (56%), friendship (48%) and fear (41%); love was most often the single most prominent emotion (21%), fear for 7%, and 32% rated it, psychologically, among the five most challenging experiences of their lives. Rated moderately or more, the entity seemed conscious (96%), intelligent (96%), benevolent (78%) and sacred (70%), and malicious to 11%. Looking back from now, 65% judged the experience more real than everyday waking consciousness (81% as it felt at the time); 49% placed the entity in some real but different dimension or reality, 26% there and in everyday physical reality, 9% completely within themselves and 1% only in everyday reality; 72% believed it continued to exist after the encounter; and 80% said the experience altered their fundamental conception of reality (60% of all respondents called the change desirable, 1% undesirable). 69% (1,773) said they received a message, task, mission, purpose or insight, which the authors coded into themes, most often idiosyncratic information (703), personal insight (571) and love (409); 19% (484) said they received a prediction about the future, most often about a personal life event (156), which the authors call unverifiable with their method. Asked in the same sitting about their religious identification before the encounter and now, 28% recalled being atheist before and 10% said they were atheist now; agnostic 27% and 16%; a belief in ultimate reality, a higher power, God or universal divinity 36% and 58% (each change p < 0.001 by z-tests for paired proportions with Bonferroni correction; no cross-tabulation printed), so at least 64% of those who recalled being atheist no longer identified as atheist (editors' arithmetic; the abstract says more than half). Most attributed lasting positive changes to the experience, for example in well-being or life satisfaction (89%) and life's purpose (82%), and 1% to 5% negative changes, with nothing measured before the experience and no comparison group. The abstract concludes that the experience and how people interpreted it brought deep and lasting changes in their worldview, and the Discussion presents the survey as strong evidence of such changes, while the limitations say that the cross-sectional design 'makes causal interpretations impossible' and cannot show whether the sample represents people who use DMT; the authors add that harms may be underestimated, because people whose lives had been seriously disrupted by such an experience may have been less inclined to take part, and each person described only their most memorable experience. All of these are the respondents' reports and beliefs, not findings about whether such beings exist. The study was funded by a US National Institute on Drug Abuse training grant, the Heffter Research Institute and the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (itself funded by a private foundation and individual donors); the authors declared no conflicts of interest. A separate, earlier online survey by the same Johns Hopkins group (Griffiths et al., 2019), whose questionnaire the entity survey adapted, sets such reports beside experiences without drugs. Anonymous and unpaid, it recruited through internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks that it does not name (2014 to 2016; dates printed as 12/03/2014–08/01/2016) adults who reported an encounter with what they took to be God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God (the purpose stated to everyone named these); each described their single most memorable encounter in one of two versions of the questionnaire, one for an encounter without any drug, by people who had never had one after a drug, and one for an encounter after a psychedelic. Of 12,725 who began, 1,702 did not meet the criteria, 5,165 did not finish (47% of the 11,023 who met them; editors' calculation) and 1,573 were excluded for other reasons (editors' sum), leaving 4,285: 809 without drugs and 3,476 after a psychedelic, of whom 606 after DMT other than ayahuasca (mostly smoked), 435 after ayahuasca, 1,184 after psilocybin and 1,251 after LSD. The no-drug group averaged 56.2 years of age and was 27% men, its experiences on average 20.5 years before the survey; the DMT group averaged 30.0 years and was 82% men, 4.7 years (the entity survey: 31.9 years, 77% men, about 4.6 years). Comparisons were adjusted for eight demographic factors but not for religion before the experience, which, as recalled, was Christian, Jewish or Islamic for 47% of the no-drug group and 7% of the DMT group. Shares of the no-drug group (809) and the DMT group (606), with the differences the authors call significant (p ≤ 0.001) marked: communication with what was encountered 63% and 80% (significant), two-way 22% and 28%; a message, task, mission or insight 78% and 74%; predictions about the future 21% and 21%; visual 48% and 83% (significant); best descriptor God 41% and 16% and Ultimate Reality 26% and 48% (both significant), Higher Power 15% and 25%; benevolent (kind, compassionate, altruistic) 86% and 75%; intelligent 80% and 87% (significant); malicious 1% and 8% (significant); existing at least partly in some other dimension or reality 68% and 76% (significant); continuing to exist after the encounter 74% and 53% (significant); among their five most personally meaningful experiences 74% and 81%, and among the five most psychologically challenging 32% and 47%; attributed change in well-being or life satisfaction, mean 2.38 and 2.26 (−3 to +3). voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_mdma_response_pr: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who took MDMA by mouth lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; a single dose in each analysed session, 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; 112 of them also took MDMA in another session after a medicine given first, which was not analysed; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, among them any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, feeling stimulated and liking, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism (rated at screening) and trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the dose with more anxiety (0.25 and 0.23); oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, impaired control and anxiety were rated on a questionnaire at the end of the session, looking back over it. For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest in the penalized models, but the association with age did not survive correction for multiple testing in the main models. Women and men did not differ significantly once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, so sex and dose per kilogram went together and cannot be cleanly separated in these data (dose per kilogram varied from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg across the volunteers). The authors note that this does not confirm earlier studies that found differences between women and men even after adjusting for body weight, and they cite others, among them an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), suggesting that women may be more prone to unpleasant effects, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people detected no differences between women and men. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times before the study. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, highly standardized, could not be studied. So differences between bodies went with feeling more or less from the same amount: at a fixed amount a lighter body meant more per kilogram, which went with stronger effects, and genetically lower enzyme activity went with a higher blood level; each analysed session had one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_meth_acute_toxic: In emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre series and in case reports, seen only through two reviews (figures second-hand; the primary studies have not been read), acute methamphetamine toxicity presents with sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings. Study conditions: a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling; in Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC and no ventilation (10.3 g smoked in the hour by the six people smoking); in Session 2, 11.3% THC and no ventilation (14.4 g); in Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, which the authors liken to home air-conditioning (16.5 g); a different six volunteers in each session, run in that fixed order at weekly or longer intervals; smoke was heavy in Sessions 1 and 2 and visible but greatly reduced in Session 3, and in Session 1 some of the people smoking stopped early after eye irritation, by their own account. Urine was collected from about 1 hour before to 34 hours after (250 specimens, including the 18 taken before exposure, of 252 scheduled) and tested with screening immunoassays at 20 and 50 ng/mL in five laboratories (one assay, CEDIA, also at 75 and 100 ng/mL) and by GC-MS, the confirmation cut-off being the 15 ng/mL of the SAMHSA Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs, whose screening cut-off is 50 ng/mL. THCCOOH became measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in all 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours. No specimen screened positive on the CEDIA assay at 100 or 75 ng/mL. At 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive, on one of the five laboratories' assays only (the other four reported it negative): one woman's specimen 4 hours after Session 2, which held 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so that under the federal two-step rule (screen at 50, confirm at 15) 1 of the 18 volunteers would have had a positive with that assay and none with the others (editors' count). At the 20 ng/mL screening cut-off, which the authors say some private non-regulated programmes use, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3 numbered 12, 22 and 0 on DRI, 6, 8 and 0 on KIMS, 12, 22 and 1 on EMIT II Plus and 6, 12 and 0 on CEDIA; 12 of the 18 volunteers screened positive at least once on at least one assay (5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session), and 3 (with KIMS), 6 (with DRI or CEDIA) or 7 (with EMIT II Plus) of the 18 would have had a screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more by GC-MS, all of them in the unventilated sessions except one volunteer with EMIT II Plus (editors' counts from Table I). In all, 27 specimens from 7 volunteers reached 15 ng/mL (3, 22 and 2 by session; the paper's 10.8% of 250 counts the 18 specimens taken before exposure, so they are 27 of the 232 taken after it, 11.6%, editors' arithmetic), and peak values per volunteer ranged from 1.3 to 57.5 ng/mL. Screening positives at 20 ng/mL first appeared 1 to 4 hours after exposure and continued for 2 to 22 hours; the latest was in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL, positive on one assay); in the last pool, 30 to 34 hours after, no specimen screened positive on the four assays tabulated at 20 ng/mL or reached 15 ng/mL, although THCCOOH was still measurable in 12 of the 18. The authors' summary that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure and confined to circumstances where exposure is obvious fits the 50 ng/mL screen, not a 20 ng/mL screen; 'immediately' understates positives that lasted up to 22 hours and one at 26 to 30 hours; and only obvious exposure was studied. A positive here is a urine result, a breakdown product of THC at or above a set level, not a measure of intoxication; this paper reports no measure of effects (blood, oral fluid, hair and effect measures were reserved for other reports). Differences between sessions cannot be put down to potency or ventilation alone, because the sessions ran in a fixed order with different people and Session 1 burned less cannabis. Funding: SAMHSA, which issues the federal guidelines whose cut-offs were tested; NIDA supplied the cannabis and funded one author; two authors are SAMHSA employees in its Division of Workplace Programs and the first author consults for that division. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

A controlled exposure in volunteers without a placebo or unexposed condition, its three conditions run in a fixed order with different people, does not meet the rule under which within-person laboratory studies start high (placebo-controlled, with randomized or counterbalanced order); what happened to the volunteers' urine is rated as a description of these conditions (METHODS §6.3), starting low. Indirectness −1 (an extreme, obvious exposure in a small sealed room, while the question is about other people's smoke in general) and imprecision −1 (18 volunteers, 6 per condition) bring it to very low, the floor. Not rated down for risk of bias: the urine results are objective, complete and fully tabulated, and the editors' recount from Table I reproduces every printed count; the serious risk of bias of the comparisons between sessions (ROBINS-I; fixed order, different volunteers) is not used, because the claim does not attribute differences to potency or ventilation. Worded as 'describes': the exposure plainly put THCCOOH into urine (every pre-exposure specimen negative, every volunteer measurable within 3 hours), but the claim's point is how many tests would read positive at each cut-off, a count under these conditions. The authors' 'rare' is adopted only for the 50 ng/mL screen, with the counts at 20 ng/mL beside it; 'only where exposure is obvious' is not adopted, because only obvious exposure was studied. The counts of volunteers and of confirmed positives are editors' counts from Table I (minus signs read from the rendered pages and from the PDF's symbol font), to be recomputed by the second reader. Status single study: the authors say earlier passive-exposure studies, mostly with weaker cannabis, also found THC metabolites in non-smokers' urine, but those were not read here. Funding by SAMHSA, which issues the guidelines tested, and the authors' ties to it are given in the statement. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.
voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_dc_benzo_strips: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read at the sites, after infrared spectroscopy of the same sample and with one combined result recorded, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples from five of the sites, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 times or more the concentrations at which it detected the others (editors' calculation) (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). A report relayed second-hand by Laing et al. concluded that newer benzodiazepines appear to be detected by similar strips, etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than other NPS benzodiazepines, still within the range useful for drug checking (Shapiro et al., 2020), so the sources disagree on whether these strips react to etizolam at all; differences in lots or test conditions may explain it, but this was not shown. Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

Risk of bias, two levels (very serious): in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants very probably knew their group (in MAPP2's end-of-study survey 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it, mostly from effects felt or not felt; MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only anecdotes); neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, and the assessors' guesses were not recorded. This bias runs toward a larger difference (expectation on MDMA, disappointment on placebo, which the MAPP2 authors themselves name as a possible reason for the 8 vs 1 placebo dropouts, 5 of them after the first session); it is shared by both trials, so their agreement does not reduce it; and its size cannot be estimated from these papers, while the differences it would have to explain are of a comparable order (8.9 and 11.9 points, lower limits 4.1 and 6.3). METHODS §6.3 rates down when the biases that remain could plausibly change the estimate materially, as here (the FDA's reviewers reach the same view, add that the in-session monitors probably knew allocation too and say the bias cannot be quantified, and 9 of the 11 voting members of its advisory committee judged the data unable to show effectiveness); that the bias is unlikely to explain all of the difference argues against very low, not for moderate (the first reader's strict reading; both second readers). voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_gen_antidrug_ads: In US youths aged 12.5 to 18 in a national household panel (the National Survey of Parents and Youth: three cohorts aged 9 to 18 from a probability sample of US households, interviewed at home four times between November 1999 and June 2004; 8,117 youths in the first round, with a 65% response rate, and 5,126 in the fourth), more recalled exposure to the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign compared with less recalled exposure did not detectably reduce marijuana (cannabis) use or first use, or strengthen antidrug intentions, beliefs, norms or confidence in refusing marijuana (Hornik et al., 2008). Congress appropriated nearly $1 billion for the campaign for 1998–2004; it bought advertising from September 1999 to June 2004, 64% of its rating points on TV and radio. The evaluation was mandated by Congress and paid from the campaign's appropriation, supervised by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, which also funded the authors. There was no unexposed group: 94% of youths recalled at least one antidrug ad a month, so the evaluation compared youths who recalled more with youths who recalled less, after propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders. Self-reported marijuana use among youths aged 12.5 to 18 did not change from 2000 to 2004: lifetime use 23.6% and 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8) and past-30-day use 7.8% and 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2), weighted percentages whose yearly numbers of youths are not printed; of four antidrug views among youths who had not used marijuana, only an index of beliefs and attitudes rose (6.3 points, 0.4 to 12.2). At the same interview, youths who recalled more exposure held no more antidrug views (gammas −0.02 to 0.03, every interval including no association). Among youths who had not used marijuana, more exposure went, at the next round 12 to 18 months later, with fewer saying they definitely would not use it (82.3%, 78.2% and 78.4% across rising general exposure; gamma −0.07, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.01) and with weaker antidrug norms (gamma −0.05, −0.08 to −0.02, for recall of specific ads). First use by the next round was 10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across rising general exposure (gamma 0.07, −0.01 to 0.15, not significant when pooled), and more first use with more exposure was significant only from the third round (July 2002 to June 2003) to the fourth (gamma 0.11, 0.00 to 0.22), which the authors call barely significant. Of 80 subgroup analyses of later outcomes, 20 were significant, 19 of them unfavourable; none of the tests is reported as corrected for multiple comparisons. The authors conclude that the campaign is unlikely to have had favourable effects, and judge the support for unfavourable effects tentative, not definitive. Exposure and use were self-reported, and with no group that missed the campaign the design cannot show what would have happened without it: effects shared by everyone, spread through friends, or occurring before the first round, which began with the full launch, would be missed. As the authors describe two school surveys, these showed some fall in youth marijuana use over these years, which this survey did not, and larger falls in tobacco and alcohol use. Certainty: low. Status: single study.

voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_coc_crack_powder: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms. A 1996 narrative review puts most differences between them down to the route each form allows and the speed and amount of cocaine it delivers, and to the amounts people use, rather than to the form itself; a 2017 systematic review names crack's own pharmacology and routes, and the marginalized circumstances of many people who use it, as possible explanations without testing them. No source read tests crack against powder with route, amount and circumstances accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed to vaporize it, while the base form (crack) can, so to some extent the form sets the route: crack is smoked, powder is snorted or injected. Once in the blood, the 1996 review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with peak levels in venous blood about 5 minutes after smoking or injecting against about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 762 people who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported more often by the 190 who had started crack (some of whom had also just started powder) than by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack: weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%, or about 2.5 to 4.4 times as often by the editors' reading of the figure. The summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for a further 93 people who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). Those estimates come from one interview, with use, form and problems all self-reported and no measure of how people differed before they started; the authors say a greater susceptibility among people who start crack cannot be ruled out, and they fitted the model with and without days of use because dependence itself may raise use, so adjusting for it may remove part of a real difference. The 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles pooled only comparisons of crack use against people not using drugs or the general population, never against powder. In its narrative synthesis, comparisons of people using crack with people using other forms of cocaine were described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies), and as showing no difference for 10 other diagnoses (5 studies); single studies found more anorexia and insomnia and less suicidal thinking with crack, and more violence toward others than among people snorting cocaine but not more than among people injecting it; the review neither pooled nor tested these comparisons. Its authors judge crack not a plausible direct cause of the infections and violence linked with its use, reading crack use as a facilitator or marker of risk behaviours and risk environments, and call it unclear for mental health whether crack use is a cause, a consequence or comorbid (Butler et al., 2017). The 1996 review, whose evidence on patterns of use comes from uncontrolled surveys and treatment, street and jail samples, mostly of the mid-1980s to early 1990s, reports that people who smoke or inject cocaine typically use it more often and in larger amounts than people who snort it (one Miami sample found the largest amounts among people snorting), that people who smoke crack reach regular use sooner than people who snort or inject, and that smoking or injecting goes with a faster onset of problems and earlier treatment; its statement that differences disappear once the amount used is held constant rests partly on two sets of meeting proceedings published before crack appeared. No comparison of crack with powder in the sources read adjusts for the amount taken per occasion, for illegal drugs other than cocaine, or for income, housing or the policing people met; the household survey adjusts for daily drinking, daily smoking, injecting and days of use. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.

Crack (smoked cocaine base), compared with cocaine hydrochloride powder (snorted or injected)

These are odds ratios although the paper calls them relative risks; from the figure the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 2.5 to 4.4 for recent crack and about 1.5 to 3.3 for crack after powder (editors' calculation from the figure readings). (2017): no pooled crack-versus-powder estimate; 12 studies mixed and 5 showing no difference, none pooled or tested by the review; one study found more violence toward others with crack than with snorted cocaine, and no difference from injected cocaine. Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and indirectness −1 take it below the floor: very low. The claim is worded as an association and is rated as one (METHODS §6.3). The three sources are not independent: the 2017 review includes Chen & Anthony (2004) in its narrative synthesis and cites the 1996 review as background, so they are counted once. Not used, following the study cards: a causal effect of smoking crack, the 1996 review's figures as measurements, its gateway reading of sequence data, and any crack-versus-powder difference in physical harms, for which the sources read give only second-hand, unadjusted figures.
voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_meth_dependence_: The US National Comorbidity Survey (1990–1992; household sample aged 15–54; structured CIDI interview) reported, for each drug class separately, the proportion of people who had ever used it who had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence, with non-medical use of stimulants other than cocaine counted as one class. Among people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (15.3% of the population; dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine are the examples given), 11.2% (SE 1.6; about 8.1% to 14.3%, editors' calculation) had ever met the criteria, against 31.9% for tobacco (no standard error; tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking in a subsample), 15.4% for alcohol, 16.7% for cocaine, 23.1% for heroin and 9.1% for cannabis. Such proportions are taken at a single interview among everyone who had ever used, including once (the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use), and do not account for people who started recently; the data are three decades old, grouped across stimulants and based on DSM-III-R criteria. The source calls the class psychostimulants other than cocaine; it includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants. A 2007 Australian national household survey (8,841 people aged 16–85; response 60%; WMH-CIDI 3.0 interview) measured something different. Its outcome was broader, DSM-IV stimulant abuse or dependence, in a stimulant class the paper does not define. Of 579 people who had used stimulants, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had met the criteria by the interview. A survival analysis, which uses the years since each person first used and so allows for people who had started recently, estimated a cumulative probability of 50.4% (no interval given) of developing the disorder within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year. The criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times, and the authors note that counting abuse as well as dependence gives higher estimates than studies of dependence alone. The two surveys therefore measure different quantities and cannot be compared directly, and neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone.

US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically; Australian household population aged 16–85 in 2007 who had ever used stimulants (class not defined)

lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine, including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription (US); lifetime use of stimulants, class not defined (Australia)

Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5). Australia 2007 (NSMHWB; weighted; stimulant class not defined; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) of 579 people who had used stimulants had ever met the criteria at interview; cumulative probability by years since first use (discrete-time survival analysis, no interval) 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within 14 years; among those who developed the disorder, half did so within about 3 years (IQR 1–5) of first use.

A descriptive claim (proportions and a cumulative probability in survey populations): starts low. Risk of bias, one level, for the Australian figures only (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); the US figures are not downgraded (JBI low; the authors discuss frame, deaths and self-report, pp. 263–265). Indirectness, two levels: neither survey isolates methamphetamine, the US class includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants, and the Australian class is undefined and its outcome includes abuse; the criteria are DSM-III-R (1990–1992) and DSM-IV (2007). Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the two figures measure different things: a proportion ever dependent among everyone who had ever used, at one interview, against a projected cumulative probability of abuse or dependence by 14 years after first use. Certainty very low. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Status single study: the two surveys measure different quantities (see inconsistency), so they neither replicate nor contradict each other, and each figure rests on one survey; the four- to five-fold gap between them has candidate explanations (abuse counted, undefined class, a denominator that may exclude people with few uses, country and decade) that have not been tested. Imprecision not downgraded: the US proportion has a standard error and the Australian 45.7% an interval; the 50.4% has none, so its precision cannot be judged, which changes nothing at the floor. The US authors conclude from their figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265); for stimulants, the Australian survival estimate (about half within 14 years, abuse included) shows that this conclusion depends on the measure and on how the outcome is defined.
voice-2026-11-13/662:cl_mdma_nonlinear: In eight men given MDMA 75 mg and 125 mg on separate days in a randomized, double-blind crossover, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.81 times higher (236.4 against 130.9 ug/L) and a 24-hour exposure 1.97 times higher (2623.7 against 1331.5 ug x h/L), so blood levels rose more than the dose did (de la Torre et al., 2000; ratios from the printed means). Clearance outside the kidneys fell from 74.0 to 38.1 L/h while clearance by the kidneys did not change, and across the five dose levels from 50 to 150 mg, with different men at 50, 100 and 150 mg, the same eight men at 75 and 125 mg, and only two men at each of the lowest and highest, the 24-hour exposure ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug x h/L, so differences between men are mixed in with the dose. The authors give two explanations, saturation of MDMA's breakdown (which they say cannot be excluded) and MDMA's blocking of the enzyme CYP2D6 that breaks it down, and state that the observations were retrospective and the studies were not designed to detect this. The authors' abstract goes further, concluding that this holds for the whole population whatever the CYP2D6 genotype and that small increases in the amount taken give disproportionate rises in blood level, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity; the dose comparison was made in men with normal CYP2D6 only and no toxicity outcome was measured. In a later study of 15 men, one dose of MDMA switched CYP2D6 off, and the enzyme's activity had not fully recovered after 10 days (O'Mathúna et al., 2008); this fits the second explanation, as does the small difference between people with and without a working enzyme (Schmid et al., 2016). The authors of the 2008 study infer, without giving a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts the effect, bodies that differ) and some take more. None of these studies tested people who took more because they felt little: the amounts were fixed and given to healthy men in a laboratory, and what they show is that a larger single amount gave a larger rise in blood level than the amount itself. Second doses taken 2 or 24 hours after a first are covered in the library's separate claim on acute tolerance.

The 75 against 125 mg comparison is a randomized, double-blind, within-person crossover and starts high (METHODS 6.3). voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_ket_near_death: In about 15,000 written reports of drug experiences on the Erowid website, covering 165 substances (reports of combinations left out; all reports for each substance merged into one document; drug names, slang and words for routes deleted), compared with 625 written accounts of near-death experiences that people gave voluntarily to research groups in the USA and Belgium (also merged into one document), reports about ketamine, compared with the reports about each of the other 164 substances, are associated with the pattern of word use most similar to the near-death accounts, as scored by a text-mining method (latent semantic analysis) that gives one similarity number per substance, with no measure of uncertainty and no check against questionnaires about experiences (Martial et al., 2019). Nobody was given a drug or interviewed for this study. With the main settings (20 dimensions), ketamine scored about 0.90 on a 0-to-1 scale, against about 0.84 for Salvia divinorum and about 0.83 for peyote and for LSD (values the editors read from a figure); averaged over all the settings tried (5 to 145 dimensions), ketamine led narrowly, about 0.64 against about 0.61 for LSD and about 0.60 for psilocybin mushrooms, and it came first with about 4 in 5 of the settings (read from a pie chart), LSD with most of the rest. Rankings made with very different settings agreed poorly below the top: peyote, third with the main settings, was about 18th on the average. When the near-death accounts were split by cause, closeness to death or how pleasant they were, ketamine stayed first in almost every subset; after cardiac arrest, LSD ranked comparably. As classes, dissociative drugs ranked first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics, with sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics or antidepressants lowest. Similar word patterns are not shown to be similar experiences: the score counts how words occur together (a word such as fear counts whether it was felt or denied, as the authors note); the near-death accounts were written on average about two decades after the event, and 30% were attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (cause missing for 228 of 625; the base of the percentage is not stated); the Erowid writers, their doses and settings are unknown and the substances were not tested; and the authors state that their analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical explanations of near-death experiences, such as the idea that the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death, although their abstract says the results support that speculation and suggests ketamine could be a safe and reversible experimental model of near-death experiences, which was not studied. Funded by public research bodies and private foundations; two of the 12 authors are at the Erowid Center, which curates the reports; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_mdma_side_effect: In the clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy reviewed up to 2024, almost all in PTSD (outside PTSD, one randomized trial each in 12 autistic adults with social anxiety and in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, plus small open-label studies and a case series), MDMA compared with placebo or low-dose MDMA increased common side effects during sessions and in the following week, such as jaw clenching or muscle tightness, anxiety, reduced appetite, nausea, sweating, feeling cold and headache, which the reviews describe as mostly mild to moderate and largely transient. A 2024 meta-analysis found higher odds of any expected reaction during sessions in phase 2 trials (odds ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.49) and of any treatment-emergent adverse event in the two phase 3 trials (3.51, 2.76 to 4.46), although its any-event percentages cannot be shares of participants; in the life-threatening-illness trial, jaw clenching occurred in 11 of 13 people on MDMA and 1 of 5 on placebo. The meta-analysis found no difference in psychiatric adverse events (phase 2), in suicidality or cardiac events of special interest (phase 3) or in dropping out, and a network meta-analysis found no excess of severe adverse events; a 2022 review found one serious adverse event related to MDMA in the studies it covered (more frequent premature heartbeats, present before treatment, needing a night of hospital monitoring). The record of harms is weak: most studies relied on spontaneous reports, no trial reported harms adequately by the CONSORT Harms 2022 standard, 56% of the non-serious and 4 of the 13 serious adverse events listed in the trial registries were missing from the publications (the 4 all in MDMA groups), and the meta-analysis found too little data on risks beyond active treatment, from small and highly selected samples. Certainty: low (for the increase in common side effects). Status: replicated by the same team.

voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_mix_opioid_toler: As described second-hand by two narrative reviews (no primary study of this was read), tolerance to opioids is thought to fall during a period without them, so that a dose that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. Neither review gives an estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. White and Irvine (1999) offer the idea as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings.
People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read

Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study in effect (Hickman et al. rest on White and Irvine for this point). The claim keeps to what the text says: White and Irvine name only a period of abstinence, and the examples of incarceration and detoxification belong to Hickman et al.
voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_ket_music: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (it says that its secondary outcomes, which it does not name, will be published elsewhere), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (citing an expert review, the authors say that up to 20% of patients given intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression need such treatment); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)

Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)

Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)

Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.

The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3), and every anchor has been checked by a second reader. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.
voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_lsd_emergency: In people who had used LSD in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (13,769 respondents reported past-year use: 63.9% were under 25, 79.6% men, and most lived in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), 102 of the 10,293 who answered the question (1.0%; about 1 in 100, or 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after LSD in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (75% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 10,293 as the past-year group. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, nothing that was taken was tested, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 102 people by an estimated 53,627 days of use (a mean of 5.21 days a year), the authors put the figure at 0.2% of past-year uses, which they call an underestimate because each person is counted once. In the companion analysis of the same survey, 19 of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after them, a share the authors describe as about five times lower (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). Saying yes was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% against 0.7%; χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001), among younger people (median age 21 against 22; p = 0.003) and among those with more days of use in the past year (median 3 against 2; p = 0.029), in separate tests without adjustment, and it did not differ by sex or by first use in the past year. Of the 102, most ticked anxiety or panic (71) and confusion (66), and many paranoia (50) or seeing or hearing things (46); 21 (20.6%) ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 (16.7%) an accident or trauma, 13 (12.7%) seizures and 12 (11.8%) passing out, none of it verified, and the authors say it is unknown which symptoms came from LSD and which from other drugs taken. 54.5% said they had been admitted to hospital, a share the authors call surprising and print without a count, noting that the survey did not define admission. The paper gives recovery as percentages without a denominator, 59.2% back to normal within 24 hours and 11.2% with consequences lasting beyond 4 weeks; both fit 98 respondents, and the editors' reading of the figure, which prints no values, gives 58 of 98 back to normal within 24 hours, 40 taking longer, 17 not back to normal after 5 to 7 days and 11 with problems beyond 4 weeks, 6 of whom said they had not recovered (the abstract gives the 11). In the session that led to emergency treatment, 33 of the 102 had taken nothing else and 69 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (51) or alcohol (24); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, 53.9% named the setting, 50.0% their mindset, 40.2% taking too much and 34.3% mixing with other drugs; about 13 of the 102 thought the drug had not been LSD and about 10 did not know (both read by the editors from a figure that prints no values). Afterwards, 62.7% said they had cut down their LSD use and 16.7% that it had not changed. The authors cite similar shares in later rounds of the same survey (0.9%, 1.0% and 0.8% in the 2019, 2020 and 2021 rounds; those reports were not read here); they write that the incidents captured are likely only a proportion of LSD-related adverse events, most likely the more severe ones, that some serious reactions may not lead to emergency treatment (for example from fear of legal consequences), that some visits may be false alarms raised by others, and that drugs mistaken for LSD, such as NBOMes, may account for some incidents. They read their results as showing LSD to be relatively safe when used recreationally, with adverse reactions 'typically short-lived, self-limiting and psychological in nature', while their own figures show 40 of 98 taking longer than a day and 21 of 102 reporting thoughts or acts of self-harm; the survey cannot count deaths or people who could not or did not answer. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported LSD use in the past 12 months (13,769; 63.9% under 25, 79.6% men, most living in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), of whom 10,293 answered the emergency-treatment question
Use of LSD in the past 12 months, self-reported; nothing tested, so what was taken is not confirmed; other substances in the incident session as reported

None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, doses per day of use and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used magic mushrooms

Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after LSD in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 20, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use

Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al. (2022): 102 of 10,293 who answered (1.0%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.82% to 1.20%); per day of use 0.001902 (0.2%; 102 divided by an estimated 53,627 days; an underestimate by the authors' account). Lifetime mental health diagnosis 1.8% against 0.7% (χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001); median age 21 against 22 (p = 0.003); median days of use 3 against 2 (p = 0.029). Of the 102: anxiety or panic 71, confusion 66, paranoia 50, seeing or hearing things 46, thoughts or acts of self-harm 21 (20.6%), accident or trauma 17 (16.7%), seizures 13 (12.7%), passing out 12 (11.8%); hospital admission 54.5% (no count; not defined); back to normal within 24 hours 59.2% and consequences beyond 4 weeks 11.2% (58 and 11 of 98 by the editors' reading; 40 of 98 longer than 24 hours, 17 longer than 5 to 7 days, 6 not recovered); nothing else taken 33, cannabis 51, alcohol 24; reasons setting 53.9%, mindset 50.0%, too much 40.2%, mixing 34.3%, not LSD about 13 of 102 and don't know about 10 (figure, editors' reading). Companion magic mushroom analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022): 19 of 9,233 (0.2%), about five times lower by the authors' account.

A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use LSD and not a cause of the symptoms. The associations with mental health diagnosis, age and frequency are univariate and are reported as associations among respondents. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it, and the authors themselves say that some who needed treatment may not have sought it while some visits may have been false alarms. Status single study: one survey wave; the later rounds the authors cite come from the same survey programme and team and were not read, and the magic mushroom figure is a companion analysis of the same survey, so neither counts as replication. The authors' conclusion that reactions are typically short-lived and self-limiting is not adopted, because their own recovery and symptom figures qualify it. Numbers of doses are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.
voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_gen_deaths_level: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 systemic vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about one hour before cardiac arrest (the reported intervals imply about two hours before death), every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributor and calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; the report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per body, alongside the separate sample from life in case 4 and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) calculated within-case ratios where a published source gave both values, then medians for each drug; the medians across these drug-specific medians were 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with more than tenfold ranges across the available drug-specific medians in all ten specimen types (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no within-drug range or interval is given, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the reported mean time to the first sample was about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. That summary is accompanied by 12 citations, but the review does not supply the underlying interval values, weights or aggregation method. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 99 entries (98 distinct labels), of which 82 have numeric parentheses, including an ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation; two are ranges and 16 labels, including THC, have no numeric value. It gives no case counts or per-value source attribution (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times the compilation's paired median for other blood. Other blood is not only heart blood, and the review's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; this comparison is descriptive, not a validated correction (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death

Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest systemic-blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold (excluding the separately reported portal values) per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.

A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.
voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_dc_fts_detects_f: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands, production lots and reading rules. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone. Because the forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS to find could enter this positive group, so how often strips miss samples with very little fentanyl was not measured (Green et al., 2020). Second-hand figures, relayed without their conditions, mostly point the same way: in British Columbia drug-checking data, 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples were missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024); and another paper relays 87.5 in 100 from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards prepared in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration, counting a faint test band as positive (the pictured strips at 25 and 50 ng/mL show a faint band, which the makers' rule, any visible band means negative, reads as negative; Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands in the main table, two of them with only a barely visible test band that the makers' rule reads as negative, and, in a descending series pictured for two brands, down to 50 and 25 ng/mL by the authors' rule (100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule), with no replicates reported and one brand graded differently at 100 ng/mL in the table and the figure (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL, from a heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024): a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.

Drug samples in laboratories: 210 police-seized samples from two US cities (2017), drug-checking samples in British Columbia (second-hand) and fentanyl reference standards dissolved in water or ethanol
Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (mostly BTNX Rapid Response; four brands in one study), read by trained laboratory staff
Earlier forensic GC/MS analysis of the same samples, or the known concentration of prepared solutions
Whether the strip showed fentanyl when it was present (sensitivity), and the lowest fentanyl concentration it detected

Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation); reference GC/MS limits 3.1 and 100 µg/mL. Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye, counting a faint band (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only, and in a pictured series down to 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL, heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024); 87.5% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al., 2022).

Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl in seized samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS and in pure solutions, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately, and the figure relayed by Klaire et al. is second-hand and not counted. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b) and adds one detection limit, from its heat sub-study.
voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_opi_deaths_heroi: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam was detected in 12% in one cited study; this is a diazepam-specific result, not sole exposure; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three publications about survivor comparisons without numerical results or enough detail to establish independent samples and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. These are recorded classifications. A ceiling for direct overdose and a floor for alternatives would be the editors’ conditional interpretation, assuming the other classifications were correct; neither is a validated bound on true causes or a measured error rate in official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003).
