voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_mdma_regulatory_: The US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, meeting on 4 June 2024 on Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA (midomafetamine) capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD, voted 9 to 2 that the available data did not show the drug to be effective and 10 to 1 that its benefits, with the FDA's proposed risk-mitigation programme, did not outweigh its risks (the FDA's final summary minutes, approved on 26 July 2024). Members cited functional unblinding, unmanaged expectation bias and selection bias; a follow-up too confounded to show durability; the lack of a factorial design separating the drug from the psychotherapy, and the therapists' unblinding and power of suggestion; and, on safety, missing laboratory, QTc and cardiac data, inadequate data on abuse liability and diversion, hyponatremia and the risk of boundary violations; the two members voting yes weighed the large effect sizes. The FDA reviewers' own briefing document, pre-decisional, had put the same issues to the committee: in MAPP2 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm guessed their allocation and the in-session monitors could probably tell it too; the only outcome after 18 weeks came from an observational visit the FDA judged not designed to evaluate durability; no study separated the effect of the psychotherapy; the QT assessment was incomplete and phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days; and the sponsor had not recorded positive drug effects such as euphoria as adverse events, against the FDA's advice of 2017, which the reviewers said limited the assessment of abuse potential. The decision itself is known only second-hand: as described in a BMJ news report and two later papers, the FDA declined in August 2024 to approve the application and, according to the company, asked for another phase 3 trial (the month is given by a 2025 commentary citing CNN; the decision letter was not read); the BMJ, published on 13 August 2024, says the decision came before the three phase 2 retractions by Psychopharmacology (see the retraction claim in this section). A 2025 paper, citing news reports and an article in JAMA, calls the vote split, and its unsourced statement that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in adverse-event reporting is consistent with the reviewers' briefing but not shown by it. The BMJ also states, without a source, that the research in the three retracted papers did not form part of the application; the FDA's briefing bases efficacy on the phase 3 trials and lists phase 2 studies among the sources of its safety data, without naming the retracted analyses or the study site (MP4) behind the retractions; the sponsor's own briefing document for the committee likewise cites none of the three analyses and lists the phase 2 study MP-4 among the 17 studies supporting the drug's safety but not among the six it pooled for its safety analyses (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The same document dates the FDA's agreement on the phase 3 design (a Special Protocol Assessment, July 2017) and Breakthrough Therapy Designation (August 2017), the final part of the rolling application to December 2023 and the FDA's filing of it, with Priority Review, to February 2024. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
The US regulatory review of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (2024)

voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_gen_dare: In school students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given; the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme), in 11 controlled evaluations published in journals between 1991 and 2002 (236 to 2,878 students each, 11,505 listed in all, editors' sum; experimental and quasi-experimental designs, the review not saying which were which), the original Project D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education) school curriculum compared with each study's control or comparison condition does not detectably change self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, measured from immediately after the programme to 10 years later: pooled d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; r = 0.011; z = 0.73, not significant), below the level usually considered small (West & O'Neal, 2004; no funding statement). In 8 of the 11 studies the interval included no difference (editors' count from Table 1); the largest, of 2,878 fifth graders, found slightly more use in the D.A.R.E. group (d = −0.117, −0.19 to −0.04), and two small studies found less (395 sixth graders, d = 0.376, 0.07 to 0.68; 236 fifth and sixth graders, smoking the only outcome, d = 0.405, 0.01 to 0.80). Four of the 11 effects, covering 4,539 of the 11,505 students listed (39%, editors' sum) and including the only 10-year follow-up, were not computed but entered as zero and footnoted as assumed. The review did not appraise its studies, names no pooling model and reports no heterogeneity; a random-effects pooling of its printed values reproduces its estimate, while a fixed-effect pooling gives d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034), so the near-zero result does not depend on the model (editors' recalculation; study estimates vary more than chance would predict, I² about 54%). Many included studies analysed individual students although students were nested in schools, which the authors say tends to overestimate effectiveness and judge unlikely to change the result; ignoring the clustering also makes the pooled interval narrower than it should be (editors' note). Every study evaluated the original curriculum: D.A.R.E. was substantially revamped in 2001, and the authors found no evaluation of the new version, so this answer does not apply to it. The authors' remark that the effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to count as small overstates the gap: Cohen's small benchmarks are about 9 times the pooled values (editors' calculation). An earlier meta-analysis, as the paper describes it, found negligible effects (0.00 to 0.11) immediately after the programme. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

The review admitted experimental and quasi-experimental designs without saying which studies were randomized, so the evidence cannot be treated as randomized and starts low; seen only through this review, which did not appraise its studies, it is rated down one level for risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), giving very low, the floor. voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_coc_dependence_o: In US household surveys from 2002 to 2016 (National Surveys on Drug Use and Health), among people who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview, an estimated 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) of those who had used only powder, and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) of those who had gone on to crack, met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were interviewed; the estimates are summaries of seven two-year survey pairs (2014 is not among them), based on the paper's unweighted totals of 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates, which its Methods describe as effective sample sizes back-calculated from the survey output (9 to 96 per year-pair in the second group). Of 21 dependence-related problems asked about, the most frequent in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine (45.4%, 43.1% to 47.9%, against 58.3%, 53.0% to 64.2%) and the least frequent was continuing to use despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine (1.9% against 2.8%, the difference not significant); most of the other problems were more common in the group who had gone on to crack, with at least one exception and one item whose estimate the paper does not plot. The two groups are not comparable exposures: the comparison is unadjusted, the survey asks about cocaine in any form rather than which form caused a problem, and reaching crack within the same 12 months takes time and continued use, so time since first use, which is not reported for either group, and amount used may differ. The paper's authors give three readings of the difference without choosing between them: people who go on to crack may be more susceptible from the outset; some may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking may raise the risk. Dependence was scored against DSM-IV criteria from people's own answers in a computer interview, in a household and group-quarters survey (people in institutions are outside the sampling frame), without characteristics reported for either group, and the item wording sits in supplements that were not available. The 22% is not shown to be the same as the roughly 30% reported for newly started heroin use in a separate study: no test is reported and the interval stops at 29.4%. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_mdma_acute_body: In 166 healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45 who took MDMA in a hospital research unit in Basel (nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies from one laboratory), a single dose raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in the same people over the next 6 hours. At 125 mg (136 people) the average highest systolic pressure was 157 mm Hg against 133 on placebo, the average highest heart rate 95 beats a minute against 76, and the average highest ear temperature 37.7 degrees Celsius against 37.4. Systolic pressure went above 160 mm Hg in 38 in 100 people against 6 in 100 on placebo, and above 180 in 5 in 100 against none; heart rate went above 100 in 33 in 100 against 2; ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 against 9 (editors' calculation: with MDMA, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38). The highest values were 196 mm Hg systolic, 145 beats a minute and 39.1 degrees; the paper reports no temperature above 40 degrees, no hypertensive urgency and no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleed). At 75 mg (30 people) the rises were smaller (systolic 145 against 131 mm Hg; temperature 37.2 against 37.0, not marked as significant); that comparison is between different people in different studies, and the difference between doses was significant for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature. Peaks came on average 1.7 to 2.4 hours after the dose. Laboratory studies from several groups, as summarized in a narrative review (second-hand), report a temperature rise that grows with dose (+0.1, +0.4 and +0.7 degrees on average at doses up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg), and one of 13 volunteers in an earlier study had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mm Hg for 20 minutes). These sessions differ from real life: people rested, with a research assistant present, in a room at about 22.7 degrees Celsius; they took MDMA of known amount and no other drug, were healthy, four in five were new to MDMA, and no one took a second dose in the same session. Heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs, pills of unknown content and extra doses were not tested, and the study was too small to rule out events as frequent as 1 in 100 (for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions, the 95% interval runs from 0 to 1.3 in 100). Four people reported no effect of the drug and were left out of the analysis of when the felt effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Everyone was given a fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in separate claims); the authors, citing earlier studies, argue that effects fade while MDMA is still in the body (acute tolerance) and that adding more may not lengthen the effect but may add adverse effects, which is their reading and not a result of this analysis.

voice-2026-11-13/663:cl_mdma_overheating: What makes body temperature rise more after MDMA is not settled. This claim rests on one narrative review (Parrott, 2012) of small studies, so its figures are second-hand and given as summarized by the review. In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers each, the review puts the average peak rise in core temperature at +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, from studies using different body sites; in the one study of 8 men that gave 75 mg and 125 mg, the peak was +0.4 at both. In two small studies at 2.0 mg/kg in rooms at 18 and 30 degrees, the rise was +1.0 and +0.8 in 4 volunteers and +0.4 and +0.6 in 10, which the review describes as nearly identical or broadly similar in the two rooms, although its own table of factors lists a high room temperature as associated with a higher core temperature. The rise differs between people: in 8 volunteers the group average was +0.4 but one person peaked at +1.9; at a dance party the two people with the highest MDMA blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), while across 27 people the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058) and there was no night without MDMA to compare. In studies at dance clubs and parties, of 11 to 41 people each and with different comparisons, group peak rises ranged from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees (+1.8 on the skin in one), the largest in 11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night; the review reports no comparison within them of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowding. It says data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, and that hydration, age, sex, genes and personality need to be investigated in people. Overheating to 40 degrees and above, some of it fatal, is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens; in a UK report of 7 deaths and 4 further cases of this kind, plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which its authors said did not reflect high doses, and in another case a friend who took the same MDMA had no thermal reaction. How hot people feel also differs: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy, 16 in 100 did not feel hot, 41 slightly, 31 moderately and 12 strongly or extremely, and the review offers as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; the review notes continuous dancing and bingeing for over 48 hours without sleep in experienced people with greater tolerance, and calls the effects of that currently unknown. In 166 volunteers resting at about 22.7 degrees (a pooled laboratory analysis), 125 mg raised the average highest ear temperature by 0.3 degrees (37.7 against 37.4) and 24 in 100 crossed 38 degrees against 9 in 100 on placebo; the test of a dose effect between 75 and 125 mg was not significant. Those volunteers rested, took one pure dose and were not dancing, crowded or on other drugs, so the laboratory studies cannot show what heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or more MDMA do to temperature, and the party studies cannot separate them either.

People given MDMA in placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each), people studied at dance clubs and house parties (11 to 41 each), and people treated in hospital for severe overheating (case reports and series), all as summarized in one narrative review; the 166 volunteers of one pooled laboratory analysis read in full as a qualifier

voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_psi_mystical: In 36 healthy volunteers in Baltimore who had never used hallucinogens and who all took part at least now and then in religious or spiritual activities (Griffiths et al., 2006; 20 daily and 14 at least monthly; mean age 46; 14 men; 35 college graduates; recruited with community flyers about a study of states of consciousness and a substance used sacramentally in some cultures, and unpaid), psilocybin given by the study under supportive conditions (trial conditions: a capsule of 30 mg/70 kg by mouth in an 8-hour session alone with two monitors in a living-room-like room, lying down with an eye mask and classical music, after four preparation meetings of 8 hours in all whose stated expectation was that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight), compared within the same people with methylphenidate (40 mg/70 kg), a stimulant chosen as an active comparison, the two sessions given 2 months apart in random order to 30 of them (15 per order), is associated with much higher scores on questionnaires of mystical experience about 7 hours after the capsule, and 2 months later with higher self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and well-being that the volunteers attributed to the session, a small positive change rated by people who knew them, and no detectable difference on personality or mood questionnaires. 'Mystical' here means questionnaire scores: on the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire, part of a 100-item questionnaire and based on Stace's descriptions of mystical experience, the seven scales (internal and external unity, transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, intuitive knowledge and deeply felt positive mood) averaged 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum after psilocybin against 0.21 to 0.38 after methylphenidate, and the 32-item Mysticism Scale total was 252.1 against 174.7 (all P < 0.001; means with standard errors, no intervals). A 'complete' mystical experience was defined in advance as at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six scales: 19 of the 30 met it in their blinded psilocybin session (10 of 15 in the first session and 9 of 15 in the second; 63 in 100, editors' sum), and the paper's headline figure, 22 of 36 (61%), adds 3 of the 6 decoy volunteers whose third session was open-label psilocybin; 4 of 36 met it after methylphenidate (2 in each of the first two sessions, which included the decoy volunteers' two methylphenidate sessions). The questionnaire on lasting effects, assembled for this study from earlier and new items and introduced after it had begun, was completed by 24 of the 30 (12 per order): 2 months after psilocybin, 16 of 24 (67 in 100) rated it the single most meaningful experience of their lives (3) or among the top five (13) (counts from Figure 3, editors' reading), against 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (top five; none the single most), and some likened its meaning to the birth of a first child or the death of a parent; 33% (8 of 24) rated it the single most spiritually significant experience of their lives and another 38% (9) among the top five, against 8% (2) after methylphenidate; 79% (19) said it had increased their well-being or life satisfaction moderately (50%) or very much (29%), against 17% (4) and 4% (1) after methylphenidate, and no one reported a decrease after either drug (counts out of 24 by editors' arithmetic). Mean ratings were 6.54 against 3.42 for personal meaning (1 to 8), 4.79 against 2.63 for spiritual significance (1 to 6) and +2.04 against +0.79 for change in well-being (−3 to +3) (each P < 0.001). Three adults named by each participant (relatives, friends or colleagues), interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session and told their own earlier ratings, rated a mean positive change of 2.42 after psilocybin against −0.03 after methylphenidate (26 participants analysed; P < 0.01), which the authors call small. The NEO PI-R personality inventory and the PANAS-X positive and negative affect scales showed no difference attributable to psilocybin (no values shown); lifetime mysticism and spiritual transcendence scores were higher after psilocybin, shown only in a figure without numbers. The experience was not uniformly pleasant: monitors rated higher peak anxiety or fearfulness during psilocybin sessions (1.05 against 0.42 on a 0 to 4 scale) as well as more joy (2.03 against 0.63) and peace (1.90 against 0.92); 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session as strong or extreme (none after methylphenidate); 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria, 4 of them for the whole session (6 of the 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count), and 6 of these 8 had transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking; these were managed with reassurance, no volunteer needed drug treatment, 2 compared the experience to being in a war and 3 said they would never want to repeat it, while most of the 8 still rated it as meaningful. The authors, who call this 31% with significant fear and 17% with transient ideas of reference or paranoia, warn that without monitoring such reactions could escalate to panic and dangerous behaviour. Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin; participants were never asked which drug they thought they had received; the monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate psilocybin, and the authors judged the blinding adequately maintained because the monitors still believed several drugs and placebo had been given. Three of the four commentaries published with the trial in the same issue, none with data of its own, read the monitors' errors in about a quarter of sessions as a sign of careful blinding (Kleber, 2006) or of results unlikely to reflect expectations (Snyder, 2006), or the stimulant comparison as showing effects beyond expectation (Schuster, 2006), although the participants themselves were never asked. The authors state that how far the results generalize is unknown and that the volunteers' religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritually significant reading of the experience more likely. In a separate randomized trial by another team, in 93 adults with alcohol dependence who were not selected for religious or spiritual practice (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; funded by the Heffter Research Institute, an NIH translational-science grant and private donors), mean total scores on the same 43-item questionnaire (0 to 1) were 0.59 after a first psilocybin session (25 mg/70 kg) against 0.10 after the antihistamine diphenhydramine as an active placebo, and 0.64 against 0.11 after the second session (both P < .001), with correct guesses of the medication after about 94 in 100 sessions (percentages without counts). Griffiths et al. was funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Council on Spiritual Practices, which two of its four authors list as an affiliation, and prints no conflict-of-interest statement. The 2-month ratings come from one study; its 1-year follow-up, under way in 2006, is reported only as bringing no mention of persisting perceptual effects or problematic recreational hallucinogen use in open interviews with 30 of 36. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the questionnaire scores during the session (two independent trials); the 2-month ratings rest on one study.

36 healthy, hallucinogen-naive adults in Baltimore (mean age 46, range 24 to 64; 14 men; 35 college graduates, 20 with postgraduate degrees) who all reported at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities (20 daily, 14 at least monthly), recruited by community flyers and unpaid, 30 of them in the blinded crossover (Griffiths et al., 2006); and, for the questionnaire scores during the session only, 93 treated adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence in a randomized trial at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (Bogenschutz et al., 2022)

Randomized evidence (a crossover with drug order assigned at random, and a parallel-group trial) starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-rated outcomes, expectation, functional unblinding) and one for imprecision (24 people for the 2-month ratings): low. Rated as worded: much higher scores on mystical-experience questionnaires after psilocybin than after an active comparison, and, 2 months later, in volunteers selected for religious or spiritual practice, higher self-rated meaning and attributed change, a small change rated by people who knew them and no detectable change on personality or mood inventories; it does not say that psilocybin changes personality or that most people who take it have a mystical experience. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status replicated for the acute questionnaire effect only: Griffiths et al. (Johns Hopkins, against methylphenidate) and Bogenschutz et al. (New York University and the University of New Mexico, against diphenhydramine) are independent; the 2-month ratings, the comparison with a stimulant and the counts of 'complete' mystical experiences rest on Griffiths et al. alone, and the plain lines say 'one study' for them. The paper's headline counts pool the 30 blinded volunteers with 6 open-label sessions (22 of 36 complete mystical experiences, 11 of 36 strong fear, 8 of 36 notable anxiety); the claim gives the blinded count (19 of 30) beside them. Not used: the 14-month follow-up of these volunteers (Griffiths et al., 2008), known here only as cited by Johnson et al. (2014). The four commentaries published with the paper in the same issue (Nichols, 2006; Snyder, 2006; Schuster, 2006; Kleber, 2006), the published responses METHODS §2.3 asks for, have now been read in full: all four praise the trial and none reports data of its own, so they enter only as what they argue and change neither the certainty nor the replication status. Snyder, Kleber and Schuster treated expectation as controlled, from the monitors' errors or the stimulant comparison; participants were never asked to guess, and the risk-of-bias downgrade already counts this. Schuster also argued that the expectations set by the preparation and the introspective setting may be an important determinant of the experience, which the claim's wording for supportive conditions already reflects. The only harm figure in the four, Kleber's 8 of 36 volunteers with sessions dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, is the trial's own; Snyder calls adverse events very few, without numbers. Nichols, who synthesized the trial's psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 282), calls the trial placebo-controlled, although its comparison was an active drug; he is not entered. Funding and the funder affiliation of two authors are stated. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_xc_afterglow: In a systematic review of 48 studies (1,774 people) of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, mostly given in laboratories, clinical trials or ceremonies with preparation and aftercare (Evens et al., 2023; AMSTAR 2 critically low), measurements taken between one day and one month after use, compared with each person's own measurements before, most often showed less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness (changes reported in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured these), and no study found group-level worsening of mental health. Bad after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked for them: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with single cases of severe anxiety and of relapse to methamphetamine use. Half the studies had a control group of some kind, but only 14 of the 48 had a placebo group with double-blinding, only statistically significant results were counted, and half the studies did not say whether they looked for side effects, so the size and cause of these changes, and how often they happen with recreational use, are unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
Adults, clinical and nonclinical, taking classic psychedelics in laboratory studies, clinical trials or ceremonies, in 48 studies gathered by a systematic review
A session with psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline
The same people's measurements before the session (a control group in 24 studies, placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14)
Psychological measures and adverse effects between one day and one month after use

No effect sizes; counts of studies. Changes in 70 to 90% of studies measuring depression, stress and grief; mindfulness; personality and attitudes; wellbeing; social effects. Adverse events: assessed or mentioned in 25 of 48 studies (550 participants); none in 11 (297 participants); reported in 14 (253 participants): 52 headaches, 6 sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, single severe cases.

Most included studies are pre–post or observational, so the evidence starts low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness to very low. Worded as an association with before-use measurements. Status replicated: many studies in the same direction for the main domains, though of mixed design.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_opi_naloxone_pro: In communities where people who use heroin or other opioids, and others likely to witness an overdose, were trained to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and given naloxone to take home (an antidote that rapidly reverses the slowed breathing caused by opioids), the programmes are associated with lower opioid overdose death rates after statistical adjustment in the only study that compared death rates with years and places without them (mostly earlier years in the same communities), and most people given naloxone by a trained lay person survived; how many deaths the kits prevented is not known. In 19 Massachusetts cities and towns (Walley et al., 2013), chosen because each had at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, just before the programmes began, state-supported programmes of overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution enrolled 2,912 residents from September 2006 to December 2009 (2,007 who reported current drug use, treatment or recovery, and 905 others, typically social-service staff, family and friends), who reported 327 rescue attempts. Yearly opioid overdose death rates for 2002–2009 (poisoning deaths of unintentional or undetermined intent with an opioid-specific code or the narcotic code T40.6 on the death certificate, all opioids together) were compared between community-years with and without enrolment in a Poisson model with one linear time trend. No community had enrolment before 2006 and all 19 had it in 2008 and 2009, so the community-years without enrolment are all 19 communities in 2002–2005 and those not yet enrolling in 2006 and 2007 (12 and 5, by the editors' count): the comparison is mostly of later with earlier years in the same communities, although the introduction speaks of concurrent controls, and no communities outside the 19 were compared. With 1 to 100, and with more than 100 (more than 1 in 1,000 residents), cumulative enrolments per 100,000 residents, the death-rate ratios were 0.93 and 0.82 before adjustment (the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals) and 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76) after adjustment for community age, sex, race or ethnicity and poverty, rates of inpatient withdrawal treatment, methadone treatment and state-funded buprenorphine treatment, the share of opioid prescriptions dispensed to people obtaining schedule II opioid prescriptions from four or more prescribers and pharmacies, and year. In the article's second model, by enrolment below or above each year's median, the ratios were 0.85 and 1.00 before and 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90) and 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01) after adjustment, with no gradient, as the authors note; their abstract gives only the first model and calls the programmes an effective intervention, and their interpretation says the effect seemed dose-related. The unadjusted death rates plotted for community-years with enrolment are not consistently lower than those of 2002–2006 (Figure 1, the editors' approximate reading), so the size of the association depends on the adjustment, which includes the time trend. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together) was not associated with enrolment in either model (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00, every interval including 1); the authors suggest that bystanders calling for emergency help, as the training teaches, may balance out fewer overdoses, which was not tested (emergency services were called or present in 106 of 326 reported rescue attempts). The article prints no counts of deaths or hospital visits, no number of community-years in each group and no test for trend, so absolute differences cannot be given; analyses with cut-offs of 75 and 150 enrolments per 100,000, and with opioid overdose deaths divided by cancer deaths, are reported as similar without numbers and without a table (the online supplementary tables, which hold the control models, were not read), and its methods name 75 as the models' cut-off where its results and table use 100. The rescue attempts are trained bystanders' reports, collected when they asked for a naloxone refill: naloxone was reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts for which this was recorded, the 3 people it did not help received emergency care and survived, and the authors expect that rescues were under-reported. The authors state that their observational study cannot prove that the programmes caused the reduction (Walley et al., 2013). The study was funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with the first author as principal investigator and no role for the funder; the first author is listed as medical director of the Massachusetts opioid overdose prevention pilot, the trainers worked under a standing order from the programme's medical director, and three of the eight authors list the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, which expanded the programme and kept the programme database used for the enrolment counts; the competing-interests statement, which covers the previous three years, does not mention these roles. A systematic review of 22 observational studies published to June 2015 (McDonald & Strang, 2016: 15 in the USA, 2 in Canada, 4 in the UK and 1 in the UK and Germany; none randomized, two with a comparison group; eligibility, data extraction and quality rating by the first author under the supervision of the senior investigator), which includes the Massachusetts study, counted 2,336 naloxone administrations by trained lay people in 17 studies, after which 20 people were confirmed dead (0.9%), and at least 2,249 (96.3%) survived when 4 deaths with unclear naloxone use and 63 unknown outcomes are also counted as failures. These reversals, as the review calls them, count survival after naloxone, not deaths prevented: the review uses them as a stand-in because it cannot tell which overdoses would have been fatal without naloxone, and it cites a ratio of one fatal overdose in every 20 overdoses (editors' calculation: at that ratio, about 117 of 2,336 overdoses would have been expected to end in death; overdoses in which naloxone was used may have been more severe than most, so this only shows that survivals are not deaths prevented). In 21 of the 22 studies the overdose outcomes rested only on what participants reported, and in the 10 studies with unsystematic follow-up only 1,973 of 8,602 recipients (22.9%) are recorded as returning for a refill after using naloxone. The review judged that take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation, but its own results call the dose–response criterion only partly met and give the experimental-evidence criterion only preliminary support, both resting on the Massachusetts study alone, which is also the only included study that used death records; strength of association, biological plausibility and coherence rest on survival counts from 21 studies, consistency on reversals in at least 15 places, specificity on two cases, analogy on other emergency treatments given by lay people, and temporality on 21 studies in which training preceded reversals, among which the review singles out the Massachusetts study and an uncontrolled programme report from Chicago (fatal overdoses fell 20%, 8% and 6% in 2001–2003 after a 135% rise in 1996–2000), from which it says no definite conclusion can be drawn. The review describes the Massachusetts result as a fall compared with rates before implementation and with communities without the programme, and calls its dose relationship significant; in the full article, community-years without the programme exist only up to 2007, a gradient appears in only one of its two models, and no test for trend is printed. The review's abstract gives one death in 123 overdoses (0.8%, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) without saying that the figure comes from the nine studies with systematic follow-up, and the printed interval fits a denominator of 2,336, not 123 (editors' calculation: exact interval about 0.02% to 4.4%). The review notes that critics argue the observational data are not strong enough to infer that naloxone provision reduces deaths, and that overdose deaths in Australia fell during a heroin shortage in 2001–2002, before take-home naloxone was introduced there. Both review authors' employer holds intellectual property on a naloxone formulation, the second author (Strang) declares funding and payments from pharmaceutical companies, including work on naloxone products, and a patent registration for another naloxone formulation, and he co-wrote two of the included studies. Which drugs: all 22 studies reported mainly heroin overdoses, methadone was involved in fewer than 5% of reversals in the one study that reported it, and the review states that its results are limited to heroin overdoses and that effectiveness for long-acting opioids such as methadone or many prescription opioids is unclear; the Massachusetts deaths are counted for all opioids together, not by drug; neither source mentions fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

People who use opioids, mostly heroin, and potential bystanders (family members, peers and others likely to witness an overdose) trained by take-home naloxone programmes in the USA, Canada, the UK and Germany, in studies published to June 2015; for death rates, 19 Massachusetts cities and towns with at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, followed from 2002 to 2009, where 2,912 potential bystanders were trained in 2006–2009

Overdose education with naloxone to take home (in Massachusetts, nasal naloxone): training to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and a naloxone kit; at community level, measured as cumulative programme enrolments per 100,000 residents (absolute model: none, 1 to 100, more than 100; relative model: none, below and above each year's median)

Massachusetts: community-years without programme enrolment in the same 19 communities (all 19 in 2002–2005, 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007; none in 2008–2009), with regression adjustment including one linear time trend, and no communities outside the 19; review: for the survival counts, none (20 of the 22 studies had no comparison group)

Rates of opioid-related poisoning death of unintentional or undetermined intent (Massachusetts death certificates, completed through a single statewide medical examiner office; all opioids together), and acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together); survival or death after naloxone given by a trained lay person, mostly as reported by participants (review)

Walley et al. (2013), full article: opioid overdose death-rate ratios against community-years without enrolment (all 19 communities in 2002–2005, and 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007 by the editors' count; none in 2008–2009), from Poisson models with one linear time trend (crude is the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals): absolute model, 1–100 enrolments per 100,000, crude 0.93, adjusted 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91), P<0.01; more than 100 per 100,000, crude 0.82, adjusted 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76), P<0.01; relative model, below each year's median, crude 0.85, adjusted 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90), P<0.01; above it, crude 1.00, adjusted 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01), P=0.06. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose, adjusted: 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) and 0.92 (0.75 to 1.13) in the absolute model, 0.90 (0.76 to 1.07) and 1.00 (0.86 to 1.16) in the relative model. 2,912 enrolled and 327 rescue attempts reported, 2006–2009; naloxone reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts with this recorded. No death or event counts, community-years per group or test for trend printed, so no absolute difference. McDonald & Strang (2016): 2,336 lay naloxone administrations in 17 studies; 20 confirmed deaths afterwards (0.9%, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), 24 including 4 with unclear naloxone use (1.0%, 0.6 to 1.4); at least 2,249 survivals (96.3%, 95.5 to 97.1); one death in 123 administrations in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (0.8%, printed 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2; editors' calculation: exact interval 0.02% to 4.4%); ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdoses cited (editors' calculation: about 117 of 2,336 expected deaths at that ratio). Deaths prevented: not known.

Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an ecological time series in which most of the comparison is of later with earlier years in the same communities, through one linear time trend, and whose association is much weaker before adjustment; and survival counts without comparison) and one for indirectness (survival after naloxone stands in for deaths prevented; heroin, not fentanyl): very low. Rated as worded: an association between programme roll-out and lower opioid overdose death rates in one US state, and survival after naloxone given by trained lay people; the claim does not say that the kits prevented any number of deaths, which no study read could measure. Revisited after the full article of Walley et al. (2013) was read (the earlier versions rested on the BMJ's one-page print summary): the rating stays very low. The full article adds that all 19 communities had the programme in 2008–2009, that its second exposure model shows no gradient, that the unadjusted death rates it plots are not consistently lower with enrolment, that acute hospital care showed no association, and that no death counts are printed; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down two levels for the death-rate evidence, which would leave the certainty at very low, the lowest level. Overlap: the review includes the Massachusetts study, on which its dose–response and experimental-evidence judgments and its community-level mortality conclusion rest entirely, so the two sources are not independent for deaths. The review's other studies support that trained lay people used naloxone and that most people given it survived, not how many deaths were prevented; its judgment that all nine Bradford Hill criteria are met is reported as its judgment, with its own qualifications (dose–response only partly met, experimental evidence preliminary). Its abstract interval for one death in 123 is not used as printed (editors' recalculation in the statement). 'Is associated with', not 'reduces', at very low certainty (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: only one study compared death rates with a comparison. A review of fatal heroin overdoses in Victoria, Australia, listed in the project's harm-reduction list as a counter-case to take-home naloxone (Stam et al., 2018), is not on file; read it before this claim leaves draft.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_xc_mindset_befor: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no named outcome measures or full measurement details, sample description or model details and its sample appears to overlap the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study read here compared people helped to prepare with people who were not, and a systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 found none that compared different preparation, sets or settings

How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks

Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).

Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_psi_emergency: In people who had used magic mushrooms (mushrooms containing psilocybin) in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (12,534 respondents reported past-year use: 62.9% were under 25, 78.7% men, and most lived in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), 19 of the 9,233 who answered the question (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after using magic mushrooms in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (74% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 9,233 as the past-year group; among the 1,895 who completed the whole survey, 1,857 answered and 6 (0.3%) said yes, which the authors read as showing that most missing answers came from people who left the survey early. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 19 people by an estimated 34,347 days of use (a mean of 3.72 days a year), the authors put the figure at about 1 in 1,800 past-year intakes (0.06%). In the companion analysis of the same survey, 102 of 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year and answered (1.0%; about 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after LSD, which the authors describe as about five times the mushroom share (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022); per day of use, the LSD figure is about 3.4 times the mushroom figure (editors' calculation). Of the 19, 8 (42%) said they had been admitted to hospital, which the survey did not define (as the LSD paper states). They ticked a median of 5 symptoms from a list of 21: anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32% and seizures 26% (13, 13, 8, 7, 6 and 5 of the 19 by the editors' arithmetic, matching the bars of a figure that prints no values; in the same figure about 1 of the 19 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm); the authors note that passing out may in some cases have been brief memory loss or falling asleep, and that they cannot confirm that the seizures were epileptic rather than triggered by psychological factors. Of the 18 who said how long it took to feel back to normal, 17 did so within 24 hours (12 within 6 hours) and 1 within 5 to 7 days; the authors add that 'back to normal' may for some have meant only that the acute effects had resolved. In the session that led to emergency treatment, 8 of the 19 had taken nothing else and 11 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (7) or alcohol (6); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, with no 'other' option, they named their mood or mindset (9), mixing substances (7), the place or setting (7) or taking too much (5), or did not know (4); 1 thought the drug had not been magic mushrooms. The people who sought treatment were younger (median age 19 against 23; p = 0.002); with 19 events, no difference was detected by sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, usual quantity or frequency of use. Afterwards, 58% said they had cut down their use and 37% that it had not changed. The authors write that the results 'confirm psilocybin mushrooms are a relatively safe drug' and that harm-reduction information probably does much to prevent adverse effects; the survey cannot count deaths, lasting harm or people who could not or did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

(2022): 19 of 9,233 who answered (0.2%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.13% to 0.32%); completers 6 of 1,857 (0.3%); per day of use 0.00055 (0.06%, about 1 in 1,800; 19 divided by an estimated 34,347 days). Of the 19: hospital admission 8 (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%; editors' Wilson 23% to 64%); anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32%, seizures 26%; back to normal within 24 hours 17 of 18, within 5 to 7 days 18 of 18; nothing else taken 8, cannabis 7, alcohol 6; reasons mood or mindset 9, mixing 7, setting 7, too much 5, don't know 4, not magic mushrooms 1; median age 19 against 23 (p = 0.002). A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use magic mushrooms and not a cause of the symptoms. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it. Status single study: one survey wave; the LSD figure comes from a companion analysis of the same survey by the same team and is a comparison within that survey, not a replication. The per-day figure is the authors' calculation and counts each person once. The authors' conclusions that the results confirm relative safety and that harm-reduction information plays a key role are not adopted: the survey could not count deaths or people who did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_gen_portugal: Evidence is insufficient to say whether decriminalising the possession of all illegal drugs for personal use in Portugal, from cannabis to heroin and cocaine, changed drug use, drug deaths, HIV or the load on police and prisons. The law, in force from 1 July 2001, made acquiring, possessing or using up to ten days' supply an administrative offence dealt with by regional dissuasion commissions (panels of three that can refer people to treatment or impose sanctions such as fines) instead of a crime punishable by up to a year in prison; possession for supply stayed a crime. It came two years after a national drug strategy began expanding prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration (May 1999), and no study read compares Portugal with a modelled counterfactual. In national statistics compiled by two researchers who had studied the reform for years, set beside Spain and Italy where data allowed, without statistical tests (Hughes & Stevens, 2010), the share of people aged 15 to 64 who had ever used an illegal drug rose from 7.8% in 2001 (7.6% in the paper's table) to 12.0% in 2007, while use in the past year went from 3.4% to 3.7% (cannabis 3.3% to 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% to 0.6%, heroin 0.2% to 0.3%); there was no national survey before 2001, the paper does not say when in 2001 the first one was done, and past-year cannabis and cocaine use also rose in Spain and Italy. Among school students aged 15 to 16, lifetime use of any illegal drug was about 12% in 1999, 18% in 2003 and 14% in 2007 (editors' reading of a figure). Estimated problem drug use went from 7.6 to 6.8 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005, within overlapping ranges that the authors say make the fall not statistically significant, and estimated injecting drug use from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000; both estimates are derived from numbers in treatment, which rose from 23,654 people in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008. New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008 and new AIDS cases from 506 to 108, a fall the paper says has been attributed primarily to expanded harm reduction, without saying by whom. Recorded drug-related deaths (deaths with a positive post-mortem test for an illegal drug, as the authors define this series in their later paper) went from a peak of 369 in 1999 and 280 in 2001 to about 150 a year in 2002–2004 and about 340 in 2008 (editors' readings of figures), while toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008; deaths that doctors certified as caused by drugs, a series that starts in 2001, went from about 76 in 2001 to about 9 in 2005 and about 20 in 2008 (editors' readings; Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Criminal drug arrests fell from over 14,000 people in 2000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession for personal use stopped counting as a crime: about 7,600 of the roughly 14,300 people arrested in 2000 were arrested for possession or use, and all police contacts for drug offences, crimes and administrative offences together, were about 10,500 to 12,000 a year after the reform against about 11,400 to 14,300 in 1998–2000 (editors' readings of a figure). The share of prisoners whose offences were drug-related fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008. Retail prices fell from 2001 (the peak year for heroin; cocaine and hash prices peaked in 2000), as measured from July 2001 by a different method; heroin and cocaine prices in 2008 were similar to those of 1998–1999. The authors state that it is impossible to say that any of these changes was the direct result of decriminalisation, and that expanded treatment and an ageing population of people who use heroin contributed. In a later critique of the two most publicised accounts, a report for the Cato Institute, a US libertarian think tank, that judged the reform a clear success and reports for an association for a drug-free Portugal (APLD) that judged it a clear failure, the same authors, who call themselves participants in the debate, found that each account rested on selected datasets and years, and argue that past-year use and doctor-certified deaths are better guides than lifetime use and toxicology-positive deaths (Hughes & Stevens, 2012; its erratum corrects only a remark on where one cited report could be found). The data end in 2008, with some series to 2009. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.

Neither paper gives intervals or statistical tests for these changes.

Observational evidence (national before-and-after statistics, and a critique that compiles further national series) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The claim concerns whether the law changed outcomes, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the trends are reported in it as descriptions of the national figures, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: the 2012 critique is by the same authors, restates the 2010 comparison with Spain and Italy and uses the same toxicology-positive death series; its new data are the doctor-certified death series (INE, from 2001) and re-presented school and adult survey figures, which enter as second-hand national statistics, while its judgements of the two advocacy accounts enter as what it argues. Status contested: credible figures point both ways on whether drug problems eased after 2001 (lifetime use rose, past-year cocaine and heroin use rose by tenths of a point and toxicology-positive deaths returned near the 1999 peak by 2008, while past-year use overall barely changed and estimated injecting, HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, drug-related prisoners and doctor-certified deaths fell), and the critique changes the reading of the death trend and shows that both publicised accounts rested on selected data, so the six-part debate box applies. The erratum to the 2012 paper (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), now read, corrects only the statement that a cited report of the US Office of National Drug Control Policy could not be found on that office's website (p. 111); nothing used here changes. Neither paper has a conflict-of-interest statement; the authors had studied the reform for years, partly in collaboration with the agency that ran it, and wrote one of the accounts in the debate.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_dc_home_vs_servi: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites, used at home on 55 in 100 result sheets, in alleys and streets on 22 and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 29, more than one setting possible; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6% as printed) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. By design no sample was tested both ways, and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from three US syringe services programme studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study, as its complete reference list confirms, and holds only for crystal methamphetamine); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study, with design and testers not stated, in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
