Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people using take-home strips and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study (its reference 66, listed again as 92, is Klaire et al., 2022, by the review's Appendix 1), and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_ket_depression_i: In adults with major depression, most of them with depression that had not responded to earlier antidepressants and, in the three trials read, taken off their psychiatric medicines, one 40-minute infusion of racemic ketamine into a vein, given by clinicians in randomized trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight), compared with an infusion of salt water (saline) or of midazolam, a sedative chosen as an active placebo so that people could less easily tell which infusion they had, is associated with lower clinician-rated depression scores within hours, largest at about one day, with most responses fading within weeks. In the first small trial (Berman et al., 2000; Connecticut, USA; 9 people, 7 of whom had both infusion days of a crossover), depression scores (25-item Hamilton scale) fell by 14 points (SD 10) within 72 hours after ketamine and by 0 (SD 12) after saline; 4 of 8 people had their score fall by half or more within 3 days after ketamine, against 1 of 8 after saline, a difference that was not statistically significant; by the authors' account mood was back near its starting level 1 to 2 weeks after the infusion, an observation outside the trial's rating schedule, and patients could readily tell the two infusions apart, which, the authors write, may have biased their reporting. In a crossover trial at the US National Institute of Mental Health (Zarate et al., 2006; November 2004 to September 2005; 18 inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, 5.7 lifetime trials on average; 17 given ketamine and 14 saline, 13 both; funded by the Institute's intramural programme, with no conflict statement printed), Hamilton scores were lower after ketamine than after saline from 110 minutes to day 7 in the analysis of the 13 who had both infusions (standardized difference 1.46, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.01, at 24 hours and 0.68, 0.13 to 1.23, at 1 week) and from 80 minutes to day 7 in an analysis of the first infusion only (18 people compared between groups). Counting everyone with data, 12 of 17 (71 in 100) had their score fall by half or more the day after ketamine, against 0 of 14 after saline; 5 of 17 reached remission (a score of 7 or less) against none; and 6 of 17 (35 in 100) kept the response for at least a week, 2 of them for at least 2 weeks; about half of those given ketamine had responded by 110 minutes (editors' reading of a figure). After correction for repeated testing only the day-1 difference in responders stayed significant, and remission did not differ significantly at any time; the trial stopped at 18 of a planned 22 after an interim analysis, and people given ketamine first began their saline week less depressed (Hamilton 17.2 against 24.9), a carry-over; its authors write that ketamine's short-lived perceptual effects could have affected the blind and biased patients' reporting. In a two-site trial with parallel groups (Murrough et al., 2013; Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, New York, November 2010 to August 2012; 73 medication-free adults who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, randomized 2 to 1, 72 analysed: 47 given ketamine and 25 midazolam; raters kept away from the infusion day), depression scores 24 hours after the infusion, the primary outcome, were 7.95 points lower after ketamine on the 0-to-60 MADRS (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71; means 14.77 against 22.72), and 30 of 47 (64 in 100) against 7 of 25 (28 in 100) had their score fall by half or more, a difference of 36 percentage points (95% CI 12 to 54, editors' calculation; the printed odds ratio of 2.18 is smaller than these counts give, 4.5). Over days 1 to 7 ketamine scores stayed lower on average (16.93 against 23.19), but at day 7 depression scores and response rates no longer differed significantly in the authors' analysis adjusted for site and baseline. At day 7, 21 people given ketamine and 4 given midazolam still met the response criterion and chose to continue in the study: 21 of 47 (45 in 100) against 4 of 25 (16 in 100), counting everyone analysed and treating anyone not rated that day as not responding (editors' arithmetic, used here because the article prints these group sizes and no day-7 denominators); the article's bars (about 46% and 18%) fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22, the people rated that day. Among those 21 ketamine responders, followed for up to 4 more weeks, the share still without relapse fell to about 4 in 10 by about the 17th day of follow-up (editors' reading of a figure; no numbers are printed). Dissociation (feeling outside one's body, time running slower or faster) was significant in 8 of 47 after ketamine and resolved within 2 hours, and blurred vision on the infusion day was reported by 20 of 47 against 2 of 25; the authors say no control for ketamine is perfect and that dissociation was more frequent with ketamine, and none of the three trials reports asking patients or raters which infusion they thought they had. The 2013 trial was funded by the US National Institutes of Health, the Department of Veterans Affairs, a NARSAD award and the Brown Foundation; one author and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai were named on a use-patent application of ketamine for depression, another author was named as an inventor on a pending use patent and had given up any royalties, and several authors reported research support or fees from drug companies. A meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials (3299 participants) of racemic ketamine or esketamine against control conditions, searched to April 2023 (Nikolin et al., 2023; no funding; one author, the first author of the 2006 trial, is co-inventor on patents for ketamine in depression, with rights assigned to the US government and a share of royalties), gives no estimate for the intravenous route alone: its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose judged equivalent by another route) includes 25 trials with a racemic arm into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more, among them the three above (editors' count from its table: 14 with saline, 10 with midazolam and 1 with remifentanil as control; each with fewer than 100 participants, median 30), and some arms given by other routes. For this category, from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose, the standardized difference in depression scores against control was −0.73 (95% CI −0.91 to −0.56), which the authors call large, the odds ratio for response 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22) and for remission 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), with substantial heterogeneity in the model for scores (I² 60.5% across all categories); its pooled estimates for this category plotted by time are about −0.6 at 4 hours, −0.9 at day 1 and −0.6 at day 3 (editors' reading of a figure), and the authors read their model's curved time term as a fall in depression scores that peaks about one day after the dose and then returns towards baseline. The review pooled no data from single doses beyond 3 days, its later windows concerning repeated courses. Its funnel-plot analysis suggested missing null results at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, which would make the early effect look larger, an asymmetry the authors say may instead reflect a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to larger trials with better-blinded controls; they also name compromised blinding in crossover trials as a limitation. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.

Adults with major depression in randomized trials, mostly treatment-resistant: 9 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode (8 unipolar, 1 bipolar) in Connecticut, USA, 7 of whom had both infusion days (Berman et al., 2000); 18 medication-free inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, at the US National Institute of Mental Health, 2004 to 2005 (Zarate et al., 2006); 73 medication-free adults aged 21 to 80 who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, at Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, 2010 to 2012, 72 analysed (Murrough et al., 2013); and the participants of 49 randomized trials of racemic ketamine or esketamine to April 2023 (3299 participants; 33 trials in treatment-resistant samples; including trials in bipolar depression, adolescents and suicidal ideation), 25 of which had an arm of racemic ketamine into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more (Nikolin et al., 2023)

One 40-minute intravenous infusion of racemic ketamine given by clinicians in trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight; given by an anaesthesiologist in the 2006 trial); in the review, its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose it judged equivalent by another route), from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose

An infusion of salt water (saline) on another day, in random order (crossover: Berman et al., 2000; Zarate et al., 2006); an infusion of midazolam, a short-acting sedative chosen as an active placebo to mimic ketamine's sedation and disorientation so that people could less easily tell which they had (parallel groups, randomized 2 to 1: Murrough et al., 2013; trial conditions 0.045 mg per kg over 40 minutes); in the review, the trials' control arms (in the 25 trials with an intravenous high-dose racemic arm, saline in 14, midazolam in 10 and remifentanil in 1; editors' count)

Clinician-rated depression (Hamilton scale, MADRS) from 40 minutes to 7 days after the infusion; response (a fall of 50% or more) and remission; time to relapse in day-7 responders (Murrough et al., 2013); in the review, the standardized mean difference in depression scores and odds ratios for response and remission from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose

Berman et al. (2000), 7 completers: HDRS change within 72 hours −14 (SD 10) after ketamine against 0 (SD 12) after saline; condition × time F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02; response 4 of 8 against 1 of 8 (Fisher p > .05; editors' two-sided 0.28). Zarate et al. (2006): completers (13), ketamine better than saline from 110 minutes to day 7, d 1.46 (95% CI 0.91 to 2.01) at 24 hours and 0.68 (0.13 to 1.23) at 1 week (drug F(1,203) = 58.24, drug × time F(8,203) = 4.15, P < .001); first infusion only (18), drug F(1,16) = 10.44, P = .005, lower from 80 minutes to day 7; intent to treat, response on day 1 12/17 (71%) against 0/14, remission 5/17 (29%) against 0/14, response kept at least 1 week 6/17 (35%), at least 2 weeks 2/17; Figure 3A (editors' reading) ketamine response about 0.12, 0.35, 0.53 and 0.56 at 40, 80, 110 and 230 minutes, 0.71, 0.59 and 0.53 on days 1 to 3 and 0.35 on day 7. Murrough et al. (2013): MADRS at 24 hours 14.77 against 22.72, adjusted difference 7.95 (3.20 to 12.71), d 0.81; response 30/47 (64%) against 7/25 (28%), risk difference 35.8 percentage points (11.6 to 54.2; Newcombe, editors' calculation), printed odds ratio 2.18 (1.21 to 4.14) against a crude 4.54 from the counts (editors'), number needed to treat 2.8; QIDS-SR16 lower by 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01); days 1 to 7 mean MADRS 16.93 against 23.19 (treatment F = 5.93, P ≤ 0.02; treatment × time F = 0.31); day 7 not significant (adjusted); responders still continuing at day 7, 21 ketamine and 4 midazolam: 21/47 (44.7%) against 4/25 (16.0%) over the groups analysed, or 21/46 (45.7%) against 4/22 (18.2%) as Figure 2's bars fit (measured at 45.8% and 18.4%, editors'); relapse-free among the 21 ketamine day-7 responders about 0.79, 0.74, 0.68, 0.63 and 0.42 at about days 3, 7, 10, 14 and 17 of follow-up (editors' reading of Figure 3); dissociation 8/47 (17%); blurred vision on the infusion day 20/47 (43%) against 2/25 (8%). Nikolin et al. (2023), high-dose racemic category, 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose: SMD −0.73 (−0.91 to −0.56), I² 60.5% for the whole model (k = 43); response OR 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), k = 37, I² 44.0%; remission OR 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), k = 25, I² 9.9%; quadratic time 0.81 (0.10 to 1.52), p = 0.025; Fig. 2 aggregates (editors' reading) about −0.61 at 4 hours, −0.87 at day 1 and −0.61 at day 3.

Randomized evidence starts high: three randomized trials read in full and a meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials that includes all three. Down one level for risk of bias (outcomes that rest on what patients report, with a drug whose effects patients notice, no check of what anyone guessed, and carry-over and early stopping in the crossover trials) and one for publication bias (the review's own analysis suggests missing null results in exactly the 4-hour to 3-day window): low. Rated as worded: lower depression scores within hours, largest at about a day, after one 40-minute infusion under trial conditions against saline or midazolam, with the fading given as each trial reports it; the claim does not say how large the effect is apart from expectation, how long it lasts beyond these trials' follow-up, or that ketamine works better than other treatments. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1), although the comparisons are randomized. Status replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.4): the three trials read share an author (Dennis S. Charney is an author of all three), and the review, which pools 25 trials with an intravenous arm of this kind from many groups, prints only pooled estimates, not each trial's direction (its forest plots are in an appendix not read), so independent replication is not counted from it; the review contains the three trials and its authors include the first author of the 2006 trial, so it is one body of evidence with them, not a separate confirmation. Day 7 in the 2013 trial: the counts 21 and 4 are printed without day-7 denominators; 21 of 47 against 4 of 25 (the groups as analysed, anyone not rated that day counted as not responding) is used in the plain lines because it rests only on printed numbers, while the bars fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22 (the people rated that day), and both are given. Editors' calculations, for the second reader: the 2013 risk difference (Newcombe) and crude odds ratio, the day-7 shares, the 2000 trial's two-sided Fisher p, the count of intravenous trials in the review's table, and the readings of Figure 3A (2006), Figures 2 and 3 (2013) and Fig. 2 (review). Not used: the review's estimates for repeated courses and after a course (which include racemic ketamine given under the skin, by nose and by mouth), its dose and formulation comparisons, its esketamine estimates and its conclusion that higher doses work better, which its own estimates do not bear out (card sc_nikolin_2023); side effects are covered by another answer on the page. Funding as printed: the 2000 trial by foundation, Veterans Affairs and state grants; the 2006 trial by the NIMH intramural programme; the 2013 trial by the NIH, Veterans Affairs and foundations, with patent filings for ketamine in depression and industry ties among its authors; the review unfunded, with one author a co-inventor on ketamine patents and two with Janssen ties. The review's study card is still in data/study-cards/_incoming/ketamine/, so the claim cannot be merged until the card is.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_mdma_therapy_con: Whether the phase 3 trials show that MDMA itself, given within an intensive therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD is contested, and the sources read here cannot settle it. Two randomized trials from one sponsor (MAPP1, 90 adults; MAPP2, 104) found larger falls in PTSD symptom scores with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy at 18 weeks (11.9 and 8.9 CAPS-5 points; see the efficacy claim in section 12) and no serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment. Against this, in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, most participants identified their group, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy; the comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, from an observational follow-up visit, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability (the sponsor presents them as evidence of durability); expected drug effects were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1) and, the FDA reports, positive drug effects went unrecorded across the programme, against its advice of 2017; in 2024 the US regulator declined approval (as reported) after its advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness and 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks, citing functional unblinding and expectation bias (the committee's minutes); and three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, including the one that set out the rationale for the phase 3 trials, were retracted because the authors had not disclosed protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site, or removed that site's data, and had not fully declared competing interests (the retraction notices). The regulator's briefing document and the committee's minutes were read; its decision letter was not. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
Adults with PTSD considered for MDMA-assisted therapy
MDMA in three sessions within a manualized therapy
The same therapy with placebo; trauma-focused psychotherapy; the course of PTSD after treatment ends
PTSD symptoms beyond the trial period and harms in clinical use attributable to MDMA itself

Not estimable as an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, or beyond 18 weeks: the only later data, an observational visit attended by 137 of 195 randomized, cannot separate a lasting effect from self-selection, unblinding and interim treatments (FDA). The trials' between-group differences at 18 weeks are 11.9 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 (4.1 to 13.7) CAPS-5 points; 94% and 75% of MAPP2 participants identified their allocation. Advisory committee votes: yes 2, no 9 on effectiveness; yes 1, no 10 on benefit-risk.

Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, two levels, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding (measured in MAPP2, not assessed in MAPP1) with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, a bias shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (low, section 12), as is the rise in common adverse events (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_gen_deaths_news_: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real BBC report of an ecstasy death in 2019; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only (about 23.9 against 22.7, with none in the heroin stories, editors' calculation), and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
UK adults on an online research panel (Prolific), June 2022; 1,248 randomized (mean age 45.7, 51.0% women; matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity)
Reading a simulated news report of a drug death in which the person who died was a man, was 43 with 15 years of regular use, or died after heroin
Versions of the same report in which the person was a woman, was 21 and had used the drug once or twice, or died after ecstasy (factorial randomization)
Self-reported stigma towards the person depicted (new nine-item measure) and stated support for six harm-reduction policies, measured once, straight after reading

Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). Stigma (9–81): man 45.6 (SD 12.1) against woman 43.4 (12.6), F(1,1230) = 11.1, p < .001; older with 15 years' use 46.7 (11.8) against younger, used once or twice, 42.3 (12.7), F = 40.5, p < .001; heroin 46.9 (11.5) against ecstasy 42.1 (12.8), F = 50.1, p < .001; editors' d about 0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; condition means 38.6 to 50.1. Harm-reduction support (6–30): age, F = 4.5, p = .035 (older about 23.6 against younger 23.0, editors' calculation; d about 0.12); in the ecstasy stories about 23.9 against 22.7 and in the heroin stories 23.3 against 23.3 (editors' calculation from Table 1); the F = 4.8, p = .029 printed with the ecstasy comparison is more consistent with an interaction in an approximate reconstruction (age-by-drug F about 5.4; within-ecstasy age F about 10.1), but rounded Table 1 summaries cover 1,248 assigned participants while the residual degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed under the full eight-cell model, so the exact test identity remains unresolved (editors’ conditional calculation); gender F = .0, p = .802; drug F = .0, p = .922. Exploratory regression (868 participants, editors' calculation from degrees of freedom): story factors R² = .068, final model R² = .569.

Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb 'increases' rests on random assignment within the experiment and applies to stigma towards the depicted person; for support for harm-reduction policies the claim reports a very small difference by age with use history and no difference by drug or gender. The participant-trait associations come from non-randomized regressions on 868 participants and are reported as associations. Status single study; the authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug deaths.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_gen_remission: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for the problem at a later interview, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window; how many recovered without treatment was measured only in studies of alcohol problems. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the table's numbers add up to both samples together, with no weighting stated). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year; many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, and a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use was more common after return than before Vietnam (3% against under 0.5%); men whose urine was positive at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment, but how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, is not reported; and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains the remission (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who had met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% did not (1,172 = 422 + 750, an editors' sum; both shares are editors' calculations from unweighted counts in a survey that over-sampled young adults and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not national estimates); in the paper's own weighted analysis, persistence was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52. Not meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). A meta-analysis of 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US (20 cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, mean 17, 15 of them recruited through treatment, and one national survey that estimated remission over a lifetime), found 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; without the lifetime survey, about 50% (editors' recalculation) and 31%. Among the people followed to the end, single studies ranged from about 20% to 96%, the top value being the lifetime survey, and this rate, unlike the rate among everyone enrolled, was higher in cohorts followed longer and in cohorts that kept fewer of their participants. For treatment, the review compared cohorts only by whether people were in treatment when they entered, which cannot show who recovered without treatment: 51% with treatment at entry against 62% without (p 0.42), the six without including the lifetime survey (about 49% without it, editors' recalculation). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figures mix very different follow-up times and so describe no particular time point, the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts, and its authors read the results as showing that for many people these disorders are long-lasting (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 estimates of recovery without treatment from 27 published studies (1976–2018, 24 of them North American; 71 of the estimates, the lowest among them, calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys when recovery included moderate drinking, 56% and 66% when it meant not drinking); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people who had had no treatment beyond a single detoxification or a visit to an information and referral centre, 36.0% were in remission at both the 1- and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% when it also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most studies used a window of about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, how many were treated is not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)

Having had an alcohol or drug problem (narcotic dependence in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)

No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment

Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).

Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts): very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and a weighted national survey) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (Vietnam veterans; the US national survey; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the US national survey appears in four places (Vergés et al.; two of the studies pooled by Fleury et al., the lifetime estimate and Moss et al., 2010, a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.), which are not counted as independent of each other. Not used: the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment.
voice-2026-11-13/664:cl_mdma_hyponatremi: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, PubMed searched to October 2019 with one author mainly responsible) has 52 table rows about phenethylamine-associated cases, 50 labelled MDMA, and 21 outcomes labelled death. The 36 rows with sodium have lowest values 101–130 mmol/L; one of those rows also reports an earlier value 137, not an extra case. Two pairs of rows appear to repeat cases, although the primary reports were not read; one case cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper; three fatal rows report neither a numeric sodium result nor hyponatraemia among their effect labels; and one outcome is blank despite a death in the cited title. The authorless 2001 case is traceable, while another row's compound label conflicts with its reference title. Ten fatal rows come from the California series, so the review must not be added to it as an independent 52-person series. Amounts are unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows. The review's single-dose statement is restricted to most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30; its table cannot verify that statement. In the 10 fatal rows with sodium, values 109–126 mmol/L lie within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in the 24 recovery rows with sodium (editors' counts). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. Faria also proposes sodium loss in sweat, while describing the drinking reports as anecdotal and the mechanisms as not fully understood. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review bases its drinking discussion on anecdotal reports, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).

Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and published case reports as described in two narrative reviews (more than 25 reports to 2008; 52 tabulated cases to 2018, with errors)

MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital

UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3 has 52 rows (1991–2018), not verified unique cases: 46 female, 21 labelled deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown and 1 blank outcome. Lowest sodium in 36 rows is 101–130 mmol/L, including one with an earlier value 137; 10 fatal rows have 109–126, within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in 24 recovery rows. Amount is unknown/blank in 30 rows, including 14/21 fatal rows. Probable duplicates, citation mismatches and unconfirmed fatal low-sodium labels limit interpretation; 10 fatal rows overlap the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the 2008 review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series, and the 2020 review (Faria et al.) is not an independent 52-person cohort: its table draws 10 of its 21 labelled deaths from the California series and contains errors (card sc_faria_2020), so it is cited for what it tabulates, with the errors stated. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.
voice-2026-11-13/665:cl_mdma_feelings: In healthy, screened adults given MDMA by mouth by researchers in laboratories, and a placebo on another day, MDMA raised ratings of the drug's effect, of a good effect and of feeling happy, and, in one study, of feeling open and close to others, and also raised ratings of a bad effect and of physical complaints, in the same sessions (five papers from Basel, Chicago, San Francisco and Zurich, not fully independent: the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers a senior author, and one author is on four of the five). In 166 volunteers aged 18 to 45 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel, four in five new to MDMA, the average highest self-rating of 'any drug effect' on a 0 to 100 line was 73 in men and 85 in women after 125 mg (136 people), against 4 on placebo, and lower after 75 mg (30 other people); of 'good drug effect' it was 77 and 82 after 125 mg, against 3 or 4. Four of the 166 reported no effect. The effect began on average 33 minutes after the dose (SD 24), peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2); in 16 volunteers in Zurich it began 20 to 120 minutes after the dose and lasted about 3 hours. In a 32-person Basel study (probably within the 166), ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (F(1,31) 121, 81 and 68; p < 0.001), as did scores for well-being, extroversion and activity, with no rise in anxiety; in Zurich, positive mood averaged 40% of the highest possible score against 0.6% on placebo and thought disorder 25% against 0, with no rise in aggression-anger, apprehension-anxiety or depressiveness. The social effects are less settled: a 'sociable' rating rose at 1.5 mg/kg in 9 people in Chicago (+19.7 points against -6.3; p = .04, which the authors call marginal) while a friendliness scale did not change significantly; closeness was rated higher in San Francisco than in Basel; peak ratings of drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ significantly between three sites (220 volunteers, partly overlapping the others; no means printed, and no significant difference is not proof of equality); and empathy and money-sharing tests rose in one Basel study, in men only on post hoc tests. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. 'Bad drug effect' averaged 13 in men and 24 in women after 125 mg against 2 on placebo, higher in women also after allowing for dose per kilogram and blood level (SDs of 22 and 24, so ratings varied widely). In the first 6 hours, MDMA against placebo in 166 people: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41% and jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), against 0 to 6%; at 24 hours, lack of appetite 31% (1% on placebo), lack of energy 30% (3%) and headache 33% (15%). Nine people reported anxiety, all after 125 mg; the authors say verbal support reduced it and no benzodiazepine was used. The paper reports no serious adverse event, depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg in the next one to two weeks, and 'flashbacks' (not defined) in 9%, 8 to 50 hours after the dose. Asked at the end of the study, 67% of 141 volunteers called the experience positive, 18% neutral and 15% disappointing or bad; 19% would probably not take MDMA again, 47% only in another controlled study and 34% perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known. Why people take MDMA was not studied: none of the five laboratory papers asked people who use ecstasy why they do or what they feel in real use (one small study outside the laboratory, below, measured what they felt); two say, citing other papers, that sociability and empathy are reasons for recreational use. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show a start that ranged up to 120 minutes in Zurich; a lowering of Zurich ratings by about 60% by an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion before MDMA; peak blood levels averaging 1.29 times higher in women than in men at the same 125 mg; and, in Chicago and less clearly San Francisco, a lower 'any drug effect' rating with more earlier MDMA use (not for other ratings, and the other way round in Basel); a pill of different content was not tested, as every capsule held a known amount. No one took a second dose within a session, so what happens when people take more was not measured here (controlled second-dose studies are covered in a separate claim). The sessions differ from real life: healthy, screened volunteers (mostly new to MDMA in Basel and Zurich; earlier use in Chicago and San Francisco) took a known capsule and nothing else, at an amount set by the researchers, in a hospital or laboratory room (22.7 degrees Celsius in Basel) with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco; in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis people were alone and gave higher 'anxious' ratings than at the other sites, which the authors suggest, untested, may reflect company. The end-of-study answers came from people given MDMA by researchers, not from people who chose it, and heat, crowds and other drugs were not part of the MDMA sessions. Outside the laboratory, one small study with no placebo followed 45 people aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub, from a drug-free session before a Saturday night out to the club and then 2 and 7 days later: 30 who had used ecstasy before (15 of them ten or more times) took tablets of untested content by their own choice that night, and 15 who had never taken it, 10 of whom drank alcohol, went to the same club (Parrott & Lasky, 1998). At the club all three groups rated their mood as good and the ecstasy groups' ratings were not clearly better (sad 9 against 20 out of 100, p < 0.10; good tempered about the same), though they felt more 'abnormal'; the authors had expected better moods and point to the setting and expectation, the comparison group's drinking, ratings already near the top of the scale and a mood list with no items on elation or empathy. Two days later both ecstasy groups rated themselves sadder (56 and 53 against 22), more unsociable and more 'abnormal', and the novice group also more depressed, more unpleasant and less good tempered (in the regular group these three reached only p < 0.10); seven days later the groups rated these moods alike again. These are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, with means only, many comparisons and no correction, and sleep and drug use after the night were not recorded, so the study shows what this group reported over that week, not what MDMA alone did.

Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory); outside the laboratory, 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub: 15 with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, 15 with one to nine and 15 who had never taken it

A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested; outside the laboratory, tablets sold as ecstasy taken by people's own choice at a club, content not tested (study condition, self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group), with alcohol, cannabis or cocaine taken by some in every group

Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people; outside the laboratory, people at the same club who had never taken ecstasy (10 of 15 drank alcohol that night), and each group's own drug-free session before the night

Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes; outside the laboratory, 16 single-item mood self-ratings (0 to 100) before the night, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later

Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses). Outside the laboratory (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; 15 people per group; 0 to 100 self-ratings, means only; Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group): at the club good tempered 85 (comparison), 90 (novice) and 88 (regular); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); 7 days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39). Group by session interactions: p < 0.001 for sad, depressed and abnormal; p < 0.01 for unsociable and unpleasant; p < 0.05 for good tempered.

Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which the laboratory studies did not measure. The real-life sentences rest on one observational study of 45 people with no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, unblinded self-ratings and no spread printed (ROBINS-E very high on its study card); they qualify the claim and are not part of the moderate rating, and on their own would be very low (observational start, risk of bias -2, imprecision -1). Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.
voice-2026-11-13/665:cl_gen_release_deat: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release (counted from day 2), and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate over the whole follow-up was 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625 to 831). The analyses by time since release used the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day (New Zealand's only cohort and one from Washington State could not): the rate was 1,612 (1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release, and the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because, by the authors' reading of their data, deaths in custody may have been recorded in some cohorts as deaths on the day of release, probably inflating the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years; 826, with an interval of 0 to 3,455, in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024; the paper does not say whether counted from the first release in the study period or from the latest one), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers, and the paper reports no check of how deaths were certified or coded across countries and decades; and it analysed only age and sex, with no information on what happened between release and death, so it says nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance and cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.

Borschmann et al. Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug poisoning 657 (332–1076), suicide 135 (36–277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Release day 4036 (887–8940), 826 (0–3455) in the ten cohorts that separated deaths in custody. Cohorts 236 to 1183; days 2–7 Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. The rates by time since release come from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (Figure 2), which the statement says and which does not change the rating. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.
voice-2026-11-13/665:cl_opi_using_alone: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.

A descriptive survey starts low and is rated as a description of the population sampled (clients of harm reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018); rated down for risk of bias and, for the overdose part, indirectness, giving very low. The main finding, that most clients used alone at least sometimes, is unlikely to be reversed by these biases, but the exact share and the order of reasons depend on who was sampled and how the options were worded. The correlates are associations from a selected model. Status single study.
voice-2026-11-13/665:cl_xc_music: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session for nine of the ten (one chose none), the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), the text reports 16 trials playing a set playlist through headphones, although Table 3 describes one of those trials with stereo speakers; one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)

No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
